docs.title: Microservices Mastery Path
docs.text:
Mastery Path BOOTCAMP VINOD BHANUJA

Most microservices advice is either a diagram of boxes and arrows or a warning that "it's harder than it looks" — without ever showing you the actual mechanism that makes it hard. This course tries to fix that: you'll build two real small services that talk over real HTTP, break the "just call the other service" approach on purpose by killing one mid-request, fix it with a real saga and a real compensating transaction, then wrap the call in a real circuit breaker and watch it trip. Microservices aren't a technology — they're an organizational and data-ownership bet, and the only way to understand what you're betting is to feel where a single shared database or a single synchronous call chain actually breaks under failure.

This course was written and run against real local services — small FastAPI and gRPC services on an ordinary laptop, started and killed by hand, called over real HTTP and real gRPC, with real timeouts, real retries, and real partial failures triggered on purpose. No Kubernetes cluster and no cloud account were needed for almost everything here. Where a full production service mesh control plane (e.g., Istio's control plane) genuinely couldn't be run as part of this course, that's said plainly, and the sidecar/mTLS mechanics are shown with a real lightweight proxy instead.

It assumes basic programming and command-line comfort, and some exposure to REST APIs. This course is deliberately scoped to not re-teach what three sibling courses already cover in depth: see System Design for distributed-systems theory (CAP, consensus, load balancing), Docker for container mechanics, and Kubernetes for orchestration. This course is about the application-level patterns that sit on top of all three: how you actually split a system, keep its data consistent, and keep it resilient once it's split.

docs.title: How to use this site
docs.text:
• Run it yourself. Every service in this course is a small Python (FastAPI) or gRPC program you can start with one command — no account, no cloud bill, no container orchestrator required for the core lessons.
  • Read the "what was run" note at the top of each lesson. Where real services were started, called, and killed to produce the output shown, that's stated; where a concept (like a full mesh control plane) couldn't be run locally, that's stated too.
  • Do the "predict, then run" exercises. Distributed failure modes — a timeout cascading into a retry storm, a saga left half-finished — are easy to get wrong in your head and genuinely clarifying to watch happen.
  • Do the projects. Each one is a real, runnable multi-service system, not a diagram.

docs.title: Level 1 · Decomposition & Service Boundaries
docs.text:
Level 1 builds the judgment you need before you write a single service: when splitting actually pays off, where the boundary should go, and how services actually talk to each other once they're split. Every example here is backed by two real small services you'll start, call, and kill on your own laptop.

What was run, and what wasn't

This course runs small FastAPI (Python) and gRPC services locally, started with uvicorn/python and called with curl, httpx, and generated gRPC clients. Every piece of terminal output in this level is real, observed output from those services. Where a lesson describes something only a full org-scale rollout would show (a real multi-team migration taking months), it says so plainly.

Prerequisites: basic programming and command-line comfort, and some exposure to REST APIs. Python 3.10+ is used for the runnable examples; no prior distributed-systems experience is assumed.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. From Monolith to Microservices: Why and When to Split: the real costs and real benefits, not the slide-deck version.
  2. Bounded Contexts & Domain-Driven Design Basics: finding seams in a domain before you find seams in code.
  3. Sizing a Service: Boundaries That Actually Hold: why "one service per noun" fails, and what holds up instead.
  4. Inter-Service Communication: Synchronous vs Asynchronous: the real latency and failure-mode tradeoff, demonstrated with a killed service.
  5. REST Between Services: Contracts & Versioning: designing a contract that survives independent deploys.
  6. gRPC for Service-to-Service Calls: a real .proto contract, generated clients, and when gRPC beats REST internally.
  7. The API Gateway Pattern: one real gateway routing to two real backend services.
  8. Backend-for-Frontend (BFF): why one gateway shape doesn't fit every client.
  9. Service Discovery: how a caller finds a callee when instances come and go.
  10. Project: Decompose a Monolith Into Two Real Services: a real runnable split, with a real seam and a real contract.

docs.text: Level 2 moves from "services that can talk" to "services that agree on data" — database-per-service, sagas, the outbox pattern, and what eventual consistency actually feels like when you break it on purpose.

docs.title: From Monolith to Microservices: Why and When to Split
What was run
docs.text: A real two-table "shop" app (customers, orders) built as a single FastAPI process, started with uvicorn on localhost:8001. Every request and timing number below is from that real running process, not a guess.

docs.title: The monolith, for real
docs.text:
@app.get("/orders/{oid}")
def get_order(oid: int):
    order = orders[oid]
    customer = customers[order["customer_id"]]   # <- just a dict lookup, same process
    return {**order, "customer_name": customer["name"], "customer_email": customer["email"]}

curl -s -X POST localhost:8001/customers -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Ada Lovelace","email":"ada@example.com"}'
# {"id":1,"name":"Ada Lovelace","email":"ada@example.com"}

curl -s -X POST localhost:8001/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"customer_id":1,"item":"keyboard","quantity":2}'
# {"id":1,"customer_id":1,"item":"keyboard","quantity":2}

curl -s localhost:8001/orders/1
# {"id":1,"customer_id":1,"item":"keyboard","quantity":2,"customer_name":"Ada Lovelace","customer_email":"ada@example.com"}

curl -s localhost:8001/orders/1 -o /dev/null -w "%{time_total}\n"
# 0.000911

Fetching an order and joining it to its customer took under a millisecond, because "joining" here is a Python dict lookup in the same process. There is no network hop, no serialization, no partial-failure case where the order exists but the customer service is down. This is the thing a monolith gives you for free, and it is also exactly the thing you give up when you split.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A monolith's single deployable unit means every function call between "modules" is an in-process call: same memory space, same transaction if you're inside a database transaction, and it either all succeeds or the whole process fails. A microservices architecture replaces some of those in-process calls with network calls between independently deployable processes. That change is not free — it trades away:

  • Latency: an in-process dict lookup is microseconds; a network call to another service, even on localhost, adds real serialization and I/O overhead (you'll measure this directly in Lesson 4).
  • Atomicity: a single SQL transaction across two tables in one database either commits or rolls back entirely. Two separate services with two separate databases cannot share one transaction — you need a saga instead (Level 2).
  • Operational surface: one process to deploy, monitor, and log becomes N processes, N sets of dependencies, N places a bug can hide.

What splitting buys back, when a system actually needs it:

  • Independent deployability: the team owning orders can ship a change without coordinating a release with the team owning customers, as long as the contract between them doesn't break.
  • Independent scaling: if orders gets 100x the traffic of customers, you can run 20 instances of one and 2 of the other, instead of scaling the whole monolith to match its busiest part.
  • Fault isolation at the process level: a memory leak or an infinite loop in one service can be killed and restarted without taking down everything else — if the resilience patterns in Level 3 are actually in place. Split without those patterns and you get the opposite: more places for a failure to start, not fewer places for it to spread.
  • Team-boundary alignment: a service boundary can match an ownership boundary, so one team isn't blocked waiting on another team's code review to ship (see Conway's Law in Level 4).

None of these benefits require microservices as a starting point. A common, defensible path is: build the monolith first, instrument it, find out where the actual scaling or team-coordination pain is, and split along that real seam — not along a seam guessed on day one. The rest of this course assumes you've decided to split; it does not assume that decision is always right.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Splitting because "microservices are the modern way to build software," with no specific latency, scaling, or team-coordination problem the split is meant to solve — you pay all of the costs above for none of the benefits.
  • Assuming a network call "is basically free on localhost" — it measurably is not, and the gap gets much worse across real network hops, retries, and TLS.
  • Treating the split as one-way and permanent — a service boundary that turns out wrong should be mergeable back, and a monolith that's internally well-modularized (clear module boundaries, no circular imports) is far easier to split correctly later than one that isn't.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a third endpoint to monolith.py, GET /customers/{cid}/order-count, that returns how many orders a customer has placed — again as a single in-process lookup. Time it with curl -o /dev/null -w "%{time_total}\n" the same way shown above. Then, in your own words, write down one real feature of your own project (or a hypothetical one) where that same in-process join would become a network call if orders and customers were split into separate services — and whether you think that trade would be worth it.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: No new service for this lesson — this one is about a design technique, applied directly to the monolith.py shop app from Lesson 1, whose actual code and data you already have running on localhost:8001.

docs.title: The same word, two different things
docs.text:
Look at the monolith's two concepts: Customer and Order. Now imagine the business grows and adds a support team that also talks about "customers" — but their idea of a customer includes a support-ticket history, a satisfaction score, and a list of past complaints. The sales team's idea of a customer includes a lead source, a sales rep, and a pipeline stage. Both teams say "customer." Neither means the same thing.

This is the core insight of domain-driven design's bounded context: a model is only consistent and only has one meaning within a boundary. Outside that boundary, the same word can and should mean something else. A bounded context is not a diagram box you draw first — it's the boundary around a linguistically consistent chunk of the domain that you discover by listening to how people in the business actually talk, and noticing where the same word splits into two different meanings or two different sets of rules.

docs.title: Finding the seams in the shop domain
docs.text:
Applying this to the shop app honestly, with just two entities, there's really only one plausible context boundary worth naming yet: Ordering (orders, items, quantities) and Customer Identity (name, email, contact info). The useful exercise isn't to force a split on a two-entity toy app — it's to notice the question that tells you a boundary exists:

  • Does Ordering need the customer's email, or does it only need a customer_id and the fact that the ID is valid?
  • If support tickets were added, would "customer" there need name/email at all, or just enough to look the person up — and does that mean support is its own context with its own, much smaller, customer model?

The test for a real bounded-context boundary: two parts of the domain can use the word "customer" and mean genuinely different things, validated by genuinely different rules, without ever needing to reconcile those meanings directly. If they'd actually break if their models diverged, they're the same context. If they can happily diverge forever, they're different contexts — and that's your service boundary candidate.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A bounded context maps to a microservice boundary candidate because of a specific DDD rule: inside one bounded context, there is exactly one model for each concept, and that model is internally consistent. Across a context boundary, models can and do diverge, and that divergence is intentional, not a bug to be fixed with a shared schema.

This gives you a concrete decomposition heuristic that beats "one service per noun" (the subject of Lesson 3):

  1. List the core nouns in the domain (Customer, Order, Payment, Shipment, ...).
  2. For each noun, ask which teams or parts of the business use it, and whether their rules about it genuinely differ — not just their field names, their actual business rules (e.g., "a customer's email must be verified before checkout" vs. "a customer's email is just a free-text contact field for support").
  3. Group nouns and rules that must stay mutually consistent into one context. A Payment context that needs to know an Order's total and currency, and must never see a stale total, is tightly coupled to Ordering — maybe the same context, maybe a very chatty neighbor that needs the saga pattern from Level 2.
  4. Each resulting context is a candidate service boundary — not yet a guaranteed one; Lesson 3 covers when a context is also the right size for one deployable service versus several, or part of a shared one.

A context map — a diagram of which bounded contexts exist and how they relate (shared model, translation layer, one context being upstream of another) — is the deliverable DDD recommends before any code. It costs nothing to draw and it is the single most common missing artifact in microservices projects that end up with chatty, tangled service boundaries (the "distributed monolith" anti-pattern covered in Level 4, Lesson 8).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Drawing context boundaries around database tables instead of around meaning and rules — two tables can belong to the same context, and one table's concept can legitimately need to be split across two contexts with different views of it.
  • Trying to find one universal Customer model that satisfies sales, support, and ordering simultaneously — this is exactly the shared-model trap DDD is designed to avoid; a translation layer between contexts is normal and healthy, not a failure.
  • Doing this exercise once, in a kickoff meeting, and never revisiting it — bounded contexts shift as a business evolves, and a context map should be a living document, not a one-time artifact.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Take the shop domain and add a Shipping concern to it on paper only (no code yet): once an order is placed, it needs to be packed, labeled, and tracked until delivered. Write down: (1) what a Shipment means to the Shipping context versus what "shipping info" might mean if it stayed inside Ordering instead, and (2) one concrete business rule that would only make sense in one of the two contexts, not both. Keep this answer — Lesson 3 uses it directly to decide whether Shipping deserves its own service.

docs.title: Sizing a Service: Boundaries That Actually Hold
What was run
docs.text: No new service — this lesson is a sizing exercise applied to the Shipping context you sketched in the Lesson 2 exercise, plus a call-graph thought experiment on the running monolith.py.

docs.title: Why "one service per noun" fails
docs.text:
A natural first instinct is: Customer is a noun, give it a service; Order is a noun, give it a service; Shipment is a noun, give it a service. This fails in practice for a specific, measurable reason: it ignores how often those nouns need to talk to each other to do anything useful.

Imagine Order and OrderLineItem as separate services. Nearly every operation on an order — add an item, compute a total, cancel — needs to touch both. Every one of those becomes a network call where an in-process function call used to be. You've paid the full cost of a service split (deploy complexity, network latency, partial-failure handling) and received none of the benefit (independent deployability is fiction if the two "services" must always deploy together to stay correct; independent scaling is fiction if they're always called together in a 1:1 ratio).

This failure mode has a name: a system split this way is often still a "distributed monolith" — many deployables, but with the coupling (and none of the resilience) of one. It's covered directly as an anti-pattern in Level 4, Lesson 8; this lesson is about avoiding it at design time.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The actual sizing heuristic that holds up is: a service should be sized so that its most frequent, most latency-sensitive operations don't need a network call to another service. Concretely, three questions, applied to each bounded context from Lesson 2:

  1. Call frequency and co-change. Do these two concepts change together, in the same commit, most of the time? Order and OrderLineItem almost always change together — strong signal they're one service. Order and Shipment change independently (an order's items don't change because a shipment got delayed) — signal they can be separate.
  2. Transactional coupling. Must two concepts be updated in the same atomic transaction to avoid an invalid state that matters? If yes, keeping them in one service with one database is usually simpler than building a saga (Level 2) to fake that atomicity across two services. If the "invalid state" in between is actually tolerable for a short window (an order exists before its shipment label is printed), that's a real signal they can split.
  3. Team ownership. Does a different team, with a different release cadence and different on-call rotation, own this concept? This is often the deciding factor in practice even when the first two heuristics are ambiguous — see Conway's Law in Level 4.

Applied to the Shipping context from Lesson 2's exercise: shipments are created after an order exists, are updated independently (carrier pickup, in-transit, delivered) on their own timeline, and a temporary inconsistency ("order placed, shipment not yet created") is completely normal and already how real shipping works. That's a strong case for Shipping as its own service, talking to Ordering asynchronously rather than needing a shared transaction.

A second, orthogonal sizing failure mode is going too far the other way: a "service" so small it does nothing without immediately calling three others (sometimes called a "nanoservice"). The same three questions catch this too — if a service's only job is to wrap a single database table with no independent business rules, no independent release cadence, and no team boundary justifying it, it's probably not earning its deployment overhead.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Sizing services around your current org chart's smallest team unit rather than around real coupling — team boundaries matter (heuristic 3) but shouldn't override hard transactional coupling (heuristic 2).
  • Treating "this could theoretically scale independently" as sufficient justification on its own, without checking whether the two concepts are actually called together constantly (heuristic 1) — theoretical independence doesn't help if every request needs both anyway.
  • Refusing to ever revisit a size decision — a service that turns out too chatty with its neighbors (reaching for the circuit breakers and retries of Level 3 just to survive normal operation) is a strong, concrete signal to merge it back, not a problem to route around indefinitely.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Using the three heuristics above, decide whether OrderLineItem (the individual items within an order, with their own quantity and price) should be its own service, separate from Order, or part of the same service. Write out your reasoning against each of the three questions specifically — not just a one-line verdict — before moving to Lesson 4, which assumes Order and Shipping are separate services and has you build the call between them for real.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: Three real local services: shipping_service.py (port 8011), a synchronous order_service_sync.py (port 8012) that calls Shipping and waits, and an asynchronous order_service_async.py (port 8013) that queues the shipment request in a background thread and returns immediately. All three were started with uvicorn, and Shipping was killed with pkill mid-course to observe real failure behavior in each.

docs.title: The synchronous version, with Shipping alive, then killed
docs.text:
@app.post("/orders")
def create_order(o: OrderIn):
    oid = next(order_id_seq)
    orders[oid] = {"id": oid, "item": o.item}
    resp = httpx.post(f"{SHIPPING_URL}/shipments", json={"order_id": oid, "address": o.address}, timeout=2.0)
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return orders[oid]

curl -s -X POST localhost:8012/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"item":"desk lamp","address":"221B Baker St"}'
# {"id":1,"item":"desk lamp"}

pkill -f "uvicorn shipping_service:app"

curl -s -w "\nHTTP:%{http_code} time:%{time_total}\n" -X POST localhost:8012/orders \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"item":"office chair","address":"10 Downing St"}'
# {"detail":"order created but shipment call failed: [Errno 61] Connection refused"}
# HTTP:502 time:0.021181

That 502 is real, and it hides a genuinely awkward fact: orders[oid] = {...} already ran before the failed call. The order exists in Order Service's memory with id: 2, but the client received an error and has no way to know the order was actually created. This exact gap — a side effect that happened, paired with a response that says it didn't — is precisely the problem the saga pattern in Level 2, Lesson 4 exists to solve properly.

docs.title: The asynchronous version, with Shipping dead the whole time
docs.text:
@app.post("/orders")
def create_order(o: OrderIn):
    oid = next(order_id_seq)
    orders[oid] = {"id": oid, "item": o.item}
    pending.put({"order_id": oid, "address": o.address})   # hand off, don't wait
    return orders[oid]

def worker():
    while True:
        job = pending.get()
        while True:
            try:
                httpx.post(f"{SHIPPING_URL}/shipments", json=job, timeout=2.0).raise_for_status()
                break
            except httpx.HTTPError:
                time.sleep(1)   # keep retrying; the original request already succeeded

curl -s -w "\nHTTP:%{http_code} time:%{time_total}\n" -X POST localhost:8013/orders \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"item":"standing desk","address":"1600 Pennsylvania Ave"}'
# {"id":1,"item":"standing desk"}
# HTTP:200 time:0.015813

curl -s localhost:8013/queue-depth
# {"pending":0}

The request succeeded with a real 200 in ~16ms, even though Shipping was dead at that exact moment — the opposite of the sync case. One genuinely surprising thing showed up here: queue-depth already read 0 before Shipping was restarted. That's not a bug in this demo, it's a real, useful fact about Python's queue.Queue: pending.get() removes the item from the queue the moment the worker thread picks it up, even while that worker is still stuck inside the retry loop's time.sleep(1). "Queue depth" as measured here tells you how many jobs haven't been picked up yet, not how many are still in flight — a distinction that matters a lot once you're debugging a real backlog. After restarting Shipping:

curl -s localhost:8011/shipments
# [{"order_id":1,"address":"1600 Pennsylvania Ave"}]

The shipment that was queued while Shipping was down arrived automatically once it came back, with no client retry needed.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Synchronous (request/response) communication means the caller's request does not complete until the callee responds. This is simple to reason about — one function call, one return value, errors propagate immediately — and that simplicity is real and valuable. Its cost is availability coupling: Order Service's effective uptime for POST /orders becomes the intersection of its own uptime and Shipping's uptime, even though nothing about placing an order logically requires shipping to happen in the same instant.

Asynchronous (fire-and-forget, or message-queue-based) communication means the caller hands off a unit of work and returns without waiting for it to be fully processed. This decouples availability — Order Service stays up even if Shipping is down — at the cost of a much harder question: where does that queued work live, and does it survive a crash of the process holding it? The demo above uses an in-memory queue.Queue, which is intentionally fragile: if order_service_async.py crashes before the worker drains the queue, that shipment request is gone forever, with no record it ever existed. A production system needs the durable version of this pattern — the outbox pattern in Level 2, Lesson 5 persists the pending work to a real database table in the same transaction as the order itself, so a crash can't lose it.

The deciding question for choosing between them, per call, is: does the caller need the result right now to decide what to do next? Checking whether an item is in stock before confirming an order — synchronous, the caller needs the answer immediately. Kicking off a shipping label print after an order is confirmed — asynchronous, the order's success doesn't depend on it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Making every inter-service call asynchronous "for resilience," even when the caller genuinely cannot proceed without the answer (e.g., checking payment authorization before shipping) — this just moves the failure later and makes it harder to attribute.
  • Making every inter-service call synchronous because it's simpler to write, then bolting on circuit breakers and retries (Level 3) to paper over an availability coupling that an async design would have avoided entirely.
  • Using an in-memory queue (as this demo does, deliberately, to isolate the sync/async difference) in anything that needs to survive a restart — see the real crash-safety gap called out above, and its fix in Level 2.

docs.text: Start the order_service_async.py + shipping_service.py pair yourself. docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real catalog_service.py (port 8014) exposing the same item under two real routes, /v1/items/{id} and /v2/items/{id}, with genuinely different response shapes. A small real Python client script then calls the v2 route the way a v1-era client would, and the resulting KeyError is real, observed output.

docs.title: A contract is a promise, and breaking it is observable
docs.text:
@app.get("/v1/items/{item_id}")
def get_item_v1(item_id: int):
    return {"id": i["id"], "title": i["title"], "price": i["price_cents"] / 100}

@app.get("/v2/items/{item_id}")
def get_item_v2(item_id: int):
    return {"id": i["id"], "title": i["title"], "price_cents": i["price_cents"]}

curl -s localhost:8014/v1/items/1
# {"id":1,"title":"Desk Lamp","price":24.99}

curl -s localhost:8014/v2/items/1
# {"id":1,"title":"Desk Lamp","price_cents":2499}

v2 exists for a real reason: representing money as a float dollar amount invites rounding bugs downstream (try summing a thousand 24.99s in floating point); representing it as an integer count of cents avoids that entirely. That's a legitimate improvement — and it's still a breaking change for anyone depending on the price field.

r = httpx.get('http://localhost:8014/v2/items/1').json()
total = r['price'] * 2   # a client still written against the v1 contract

raw v2 response: {'id': 1, 'title': 'Desk Lamp', 'price_cents': 2499}
client written for v1 broke on v2 response: KeyError 'price'

That's a real KeyError, not a hypothetical one. If Catalog Service had simply changed /items/{id} in place instead of adding a new versioned route, every existing caller depending on price would break the moment the new code deployed — with no coordination point, no warning, and no rollback path short of reverting the deploy.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A REST contract is everything a caller can depend on: the URL shape, the HTTP methods allowed, required and optional request fields, response field names and types, status codes used for each outcome, and (often forgotten) the error response shape. Any change to this contract falls into one of two categories:

  • Additive / backward-compatible: adding a new optional request field, adding a new response field a client can simply ignore, adding a new endpoint. Existing clients, written before the change, keep working unmodified.
  • Breaking: renaming or removing a field, changing a field's type or meaning, changing a status code's meaning, tightening validation on an existing field. Existing clients may start failing, exactly as shown above.

Because microservices deploy independently, a breaking change to a contract cannot be coordinated with "redeploy the client at the same time" the way it sometimes can inside a monolith's single deploy. The practical techniques to survive this, roughly in order of how much they cost to maintain:

  1. Never break a contract once published — only add. This is the cheapest long-term policy but requires discipline (e.g., representing the v1→v2 cents change as an additional field, price_cents, added alongside the old price, rather than a replacement) and isn't always possible (a genuinely wrong field can't be fixed this way forever).
  2. URL or header versioning — /v1/... vs /v2/... (what this demo uses) or an Accept: application/vnd.shop.v2+json header. Both versions are live simultaneously; old clients keep calling /v1 indefinitely while new clients adopt /v2, and /v1 is only removed once telemetry shows nothing is calling it anymore.
  3. Consumer-driven contract testing — covered in depth in Level 3, Lesson 9 — catches a contract-breaking change in CI, before it deploys, by running the provider's new code against the actual expectations each real consumer has recorded.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating "backward compatible" as a feeling instead of a checklist — renaming a field is breaking even if the new name is "obviously better"; removing a field a client might not be using is still breaking for the client that is.
  • Versioning the whole service instead of the specific contract that changed, forcing every consumer to re-integrate for a change that only affected one endpoint.
  • Never retiring an old version — if /v1 is kept alive "just in case" forever with no usage telemetry, every future contract change has to consider two live surfaces instead of one, indefinitely.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real .proto contract compiled with grpc_tools.protoc into real generated Python stubs, a real gRPC server on port 50051, and a real client calling it — including one call for an item that doesn't exist, producing a real NOT_FOUND status. Then a real 200-call timing comparison against the REST catalog_service.py from Lesson 5, both running locally.

docs.title: The contract, compiled, not just documented
docs.text:
service Inventory {
  rpc GetStock (StockRequest) returns (StockReply);
}
message StockRequest { int32 item_id = 1; }
message StockReply { int32 item_id = 1; int32 quantity_available = 2; }

python -m grpc_tools.protoc -I. --python_out=. --grpc_python_out=. inventory.proto
# generates inventory_pb2.py and inventory_pb2_grpc.py

Unlike the REST contract in Lesson 5 — which lived only as convention and documentation until a client broke against it — this contract is compiled into real Python classes. A client calling inventory_pb2.StockRequest(item_id="x") with a string instead of an int fails immediately, locally, with a type error, before any network call happens.

python client.py 1
# item_id=1 quantity_available=42
python client.py 2
# item_id=2 quantity_available=0
python client.py 999
# RPC failed: code=StatusCode.NOT_FOUND details=item 999 not found

That NOT_FOUND is a real gRPC status code (context.set_code(grpc.StatusCode.NOT_FOUND) on the server), the gRPC equivalent of an HTTP 404 — but delivered as a structured, typed error the client catches as grpc.RpcError, not a JSON body the client has to parse and hope matches a documented error shape.

docs.title: The real latency difference
docs.text:
# 200 gRPC calls: 0.0300s total, 0.150ms/call
# 200 REST calls: 0.1799s total, 0.899ms/call

On this machine, for this tiny payload, gRPC was about 6x faster per call than REST/JSON over HTTP/1.1. That gap comes from two real, specific mechanisms, not "gRPC is just faster":

  1. Binary Protocol Buffers vs. text JSON. Encoding {"item_id": 1, "quantity_available": 42} as JSON means parsing a text format with field names repeated on every message. Protobuf encodes the same data as a compact binary blob with field numbers, not names, and a schema both sides already agree on.
  2. HTTP/2 multiplexing vs. HTTP/1.1. gRPC runs on HTTP/2, which can multiplex many requests over one connection; the REST call here used httpx.Client(), which reuses a connection but still pays HTTP/1.1's per-request overhead.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
gRPC is built on three pieces that work together: Protocol Buffers for the wire format and schema, HTTP/2 for transport, and generated client/server code so neither side hand-writes serialization logic. The schema (inventory.proto) is the single source of truth both services compile against — a genuine advantage over REST, where the "schema" is usually just a shared understanding (or an OpenAPI doc that can silently drift from the real behavior).

This makes gRPC a strong default for internal, service-to-service calls where both ends are services you control and can recompile together: the type safety and performance both pay off, and nobody outside your system needs to read the wire format directly. It's a weaker fit for public-facing APIs: browsers can't easily call gRPC without a proxy layer (grpc-web), and external developers generally expect to read and test a JSON/REST API with curl or Postman without installing your .proto files and a code generator first. Many real systems use both: gRPC between internal services, REST (or GraphQL) at the edge facing browsers and third parties — which is exactly why the API Gateway pattern in the next lesson matters: something has to translate between the two worlds.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Choosing gRPC for a public API because it's faster, then discovering browsers and casual API consumers can't call it directly without extra infrastructure (grpc-web, a REST-to-gRPC gateway).
  • Changing a .proto field's number or type instead of only adding new fields with new numbers — protobuf's wire compatibility rules are stricter and less forgiving than JSON's "extra fields are ignored," and a mismatched field number silently reads the wrong data instead of erroring.
  • Assuming the 6x speedup measured here holds at every payload size — for very large payloads, serialization format matters less than the payload size itself, and the gap narrows.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real gateway.py FastAPI service (port 8015) that calls two real downstream services for a single client request: the REST catalog_service.py from Lesson 5 and the gRPC Inventory service from Lesson 6. All three were running locally and called with real curl requests.

docs.title: One client call, two backends, one response — and a real gotcha
docs.text:
@app.get("/api/items/{item_id}")
def get_item(item_id: int):
    catalog = httpx.get(f"{CATALOG_URL}/v2/items/{item_id}").raise_for_status().json()
    stock = inventory_stub.GetStock(StockRequest(item_id=item_id))  # gRPC, different protocol entirely
    return {"id": catalog["id"], "title": catalog["title"], "price_cents": catalog["price_cents"],
            "in_stock": stock.quantity_available > 0, "quantity_available": stock.quantity_available}

curl -s localhost:8015/api/items/1
# {"id":1,"title":"Desk Lamp","price_cents":2499,"in_stock":true,"quantity_available":42}

curl -s localhost:8015/api/items/2
# {"detail":"catalog service unavailable"}

Item 2 exists in the gRPC Inventory service (with quantity 0) but not in Catalog Service's items dict. The gateway's response for it is "catalog service unavailable" — which is not what actually happened. Checking directly:

curl -s -w "\nHTTP:%{http_code}\n" localhost:8014/v2/items/2
# Internal Server Error
# HTTP:500

Catalog Service was fully up; it just has an unhandled KeyError for an item ID it doesn't know (items[item_id] with no existence check), which FastAPI turns into a generic 500. The gateway's except httpx.HTTPError catches both a real connection failure and this unrelated 500 the same way, because httpx.HTTPStatusError (raised by raise_for_status() on any 4xx/5xx) is itself a subclass of httpx.HTTPError. The gateway collapsed two genuinely different failures — "the service is down" and "the service is up but this specific request is invalid" — into one indistinguishable, misleading message. This is a real, common gateway bug, not a contrived one.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
An API Gateway sits between external callers and a set of internal services, and does some combination of: routing a request to the right backend service, aggregating multiple backend calls into one response (as above), translating between protocols (REST in, gRPC to a backend, as above), and cross-cutting concerns like authentication, rate limiting, and request logging that would otherwise need to be duplicated in every service.

Its real value is hiding internal topology from external callers — a caller of /api/items/1 doesn't need to know Catalog is REST and Inventory is gRPC, or that they're two different processes at all. Its real cost, demonstrated above, is that the gateway becomes responsible for correctly interpreting every backend's failure modes, and getting that wrong (as this demo's gateway did) produces a worse debugging experience than calling each backend directly would have — the client sees "unavailable" when the truth is "backend returned a 500 for this specific input," two very different problems requiring different fixes.

The correct fix, which real gateways implement, is to distinguish failure types explicitly rather than catching one broad exception class:

try:
    catalog_resp = httpx.get(...)
    catalog_resp.raise_for_status()
except httpx.ConnectError:
    raise HTTPException(503, "catalog service unreachable")
except httpx.HTTPStatusError as e:
    raise HTTPException(e.response.status_code, f"catalog service returned {e.response.status_code}")

This is also the architectural argument for the Backend-for-Frontend pattern (next lesson): a single generic gateway trying to serve every client type and hide every backend's quirks accumulates exactly this kind of lossy error-translation logic, multiplied across every route.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Catching a broad exception type at the gateway and translating every case to the same generic error, exactly as this demo did — always distinguish "couldn't reach the backend" from "backend responded with an error" from "backend responded successfully with data the gateway can't parse."
  • Putting business logic (not just routing/aggregation/translation) in the gateway — a gateway that decides discount rules or validates domain rules becomes a second place those rules live, and the two copies drift.
  • Making the gateway a single point of failure with no redundancy — since literally every client request flows through it, it needs the same (or better) availability engineering as the services behind it.

Separately, fix the root cause in catalog_service.py by raising a proper 404 for an unknown item_id instead of letting the KeyError propagate.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: Two real FastAPI services, mobile_bff.py (port 8016) and web_bff.py (port 8017), each calling the same catalog_service.py from Lesson 5 and shaping the response differently for its client type. Response sizes below are real byte counts from curl ... | wc -c.

docs.title: Same data, two shapes
docs.text:
# mobile_bff.py — compact card, no raw cents, truncated title
return {"id": i["id"], "t": i["title"][:20], "price_display": f"${i['price_cents']/100:.2f}"}

# web_bff.py — full title, raw cents for client formatting, plus SEO metadata mobile never needs
return {"id": i["id"], "title": i["title"], "price_cents": i["price_cents"],
        "seo": {"meta_title": f"{i['title']} | Shop", "meta_description": f"Buy {i['title']} today."}}

curl -s localhost:8016/mobile/items/1
# {"id":1,"t":"Desk Lamp","price_display":"$24.99"}
curl -s localhost:8017/web/items/1
# {"id":1,"title":"Desk Lamp","price_cents":2499,"seo":{"meta_title":"Desk Lamp | Shop","meta_description":"Buy Desk Lamp today."}}

curl -s localhost:8016/mobile/items/1 | wc -c   #  49
curl -s localhost:8017/web/items/1   | wc -c   # 129

The web response is 2.6x the byte size of the mobile one for the exact same underlying item, because it carries SEO metadata that only matters to a server-rendered web page, not a mobile app. On a slow mobile connection, that difference is a real, user-visible latency cost if mobile had to download and discard the SEO fields it doesn't use.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The single generic API Gateway from the previous lesson has a scaling problem that only shows up once you have more than one kind of client: a mobile app, a web app, and maybe a third-party partner integration each want different shapes of the same underlying data — different fields, different levels of detail, different aggregations. A single gateway trying to serve all of them accumulates either:

  • One bloated endpoint returning the union of every field every client might ever want (the web BFF's shape, served to mobile too) — correct, but wasteful, exactly as measured above.
  • A pile of if client_type == "mobile" branches inside one endpoint — correct, but every client's logic is now tangled together in one file, owned by whichever team touches it last.

The Backend-for-Frontend pattern resolves this by giving each client type (or each client team) its own gateway, each calling the same underlying services but shaping, filtering, and aggregating the response exactly for that one client. The mobile team owns and evolves mobile_bff.py without needing sign-off from the web team, and vice versa — each BFF's release cadence matches its client's release cadence (a mobile app update is slow and app-store-gated; a web frontend deploys continuously), which a single shared gateway can't do without one team's urgency blocking the other's stability.

The cost is real too: logic that's genuinely shared across clients (auth, the error-translation fix from Lesson 7) now has to be duplicated or factored into a shared library across every BFF, and you've traded "N endpoints in one gateway" for "N gateways," each needing its own deployment and monitoring.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Creating a BFF per client platform when the real difference is per client team — two teams building for the same platform with genuinely different needs is a better BFF boundary than "iOS gets one, Android gets one" if both actually want the same shape.
  • Letting business logic (not just response shaping) live in a BFF — a discount calculation implemented differently in mobile_bff.py and web_bff.py is the same "two copies of the truth" problem called out in Lesson 7, just multiplied by the number of BFFs.
  • Skipping the shared error-handling fix from Lesson 7 in each BFF independently — without a shared library, each BFF can reintroduce the same "unavailable" bug on its own.
