Run it alongside the other two, confirm its response is smaller than both, and write one sentence on why a partner integration's data needs might diverge from both a mobile app's and a web app's.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real registry.py service (port 8019) that instances register with and heartbeat every 3 seconds, a real gateway_discovery.py (port 8018) that looks up catalog's current address instead of hardcoding it, and a real catalog_discoverable.py instance moved from port 8020 to port 8021 mid-course, with the old instance actually killed, to see exactly how the gateway reacts.

docs.title: Starting an instance, and watching it register itself
docs.text:
def heartbeat():
    while True:
        httpx.post(f"{REGISTRY_URL}/register", json={"name": "catalog", "url": f"http://localhost:{PORT}"})
        time.sleep(3)

curl -s localhost:8019/instances
# {"catalog":{"url":"http://localhost:8020","last_heartbeat":1792950498.89}}

curl -s localhost:8018/items/1
# {"id":1,"title":"Desk Lamp","price_cents":2499}

The gateway never hardcodes http://localhost:8020 — it asks the registry "where is catalog right now?" on every request (httpx.get(f"{REGISTRY_URL}/lookup/catalog")), then calls whatever URL comes back.

docs.title: Killing the instance exposes a real gap
docs.text:
pkill -f "catalog_discoverable.py 8020"
curl -s -w "\nHTTP:%{http_code}\n" localhost:8018/items/1
# Internal Server Error
# HTTP:500

This 500 is real, and it reveals something this simple registry does not solve: the registry only learns an instance is dead when its heartbeat stops arriving for TTL_SECONDS (10s here). In the gap between the kill and the TTL expiry, lookup/catalog keeps returning the now-dead URL as if it were healthy, and the gateway's own httpx.get(catalog_url...) call fails with an uncaught connection error, which FastAPI turns into a generic 500 — the exact kind of swallowed, unhelpful error Lesson 7 warned about.

Starting a new instance on a different port fixes it immediately, because registration is push-based, not discovery-based from a fixed list:

python catalog_discoverable.py 8021   # new port, same service name
curl -s localhost:8019/instances
# {"catalog":{"url":"http://localhost:8021","last_heartbeat":1792950515.64}}
curl -s localhost:8018/items/1
# {"id":1,"title":"Desk Lamp","price_cents":2499}

No gateway code changed, no gateway restart happened — it picked up port 8021 automatically on the very next request, because it never knew about 8020 in the first place; it only ever asked the registry.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Hardcoding a downstream service's address (CATALOG_URL = "http://localhost:8014", as every earlier lesson in this level did) works fine with exactly one instance that never moves. It breaks down the moment you have more than one instance of a service (for load distribution) or instances that come and go (deploys, autoscaling, crashes and restarts) — which is normal, expected behavior in any real microservices deployment, not an edge case.

Service discovery solves this with one of two general approaches:

  • Client-side discovery (what this demo built): each service instance registers itself with a shared registry on startup and re-registers (heartbeats) periodically; callers query the registry before each call, or cache the result briefly. This is roughly how tools like Consul or etcd-backed discovery work, and roughly what Kubernetes' own internal DNS-based service discovery abstracts away for you (a Kubernetes Service is a registry, with the kubelet handling the heartbeat-equivalent health checking).
  • Server-side discovery: callers always talk to a fixed address (a load balancer), and the load balancer itself queries the registry and routes to a healthy instance. The caller never touches the registry directly.

The real gap this demo exposed — a TTL-based registry has a window where it confidently returns a dead address — is not a bug unique to this toy implementation; it's the fundamental reason production discovery systems pair registration with active health checks (the registry or load balancer itself pings each registered instance, rather than only trusting self-reported heartbeats) and short TTLs, trading faster dead-instance detection against more overhead. Kubernetes' readiness/liveness probes exist for exactly this reason.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Trusting only self-reported heartbeats (as this demo does) in a system where an instance might hang rather than cleanly die — a hung process can keep its heartbeat thread alive while failing every real request.
  • Setting the TTL too long "to reduce registry load," which widens the stale-address window demonstrated above; or too short, which can deregister a healthy instance during a brief GC pause or network blip.
  • Building a custom registry like this one for production use instead of reaching for an existing, battle-tested system (Kubernetes Services, Consul, etcd) — this demo is deliberately minimal to show the mechanism, not something to actually deploy.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add an active health check to registry.py: a background thread that, every 5 seconds, sends a real HTTP request to each registered instance's /items/1 endpoint and removes any registration that fails to respond, independent of whether its heartbeat is still arriving on time. Kill a catalog instance with kill -9 (not a graceful shutdown) and measure, with real timestamps, how much faster this active check detects the dead instance compared to waiting for the 10-second heartbeat TTL alone.

docs.title: Project: Decompose a Monolith Into Two Real Services
What was run
docs.text: The monolith.py shop app from Lesson 1 was split into two real, independently running services — customers_service.py (port 8031) and orders_service.py (port 8032) — with the former in-process dict lookup replaced by a real httpx call between them. Every number and error below is real, observed output from these two running processes.

docs.title: The split, and what it actually cost
docs.text:
# orders_service.py — the join that was one line in monolith.py is now a network call
@app.get("/orders/{oid}")
def get_order(oid: int):
    order = orders[oid]
    r = httpx.get(f"{CUSTOMERS_URL}/customers/{order['customer_id']}", timeout=2.0)
    customer = r.json()
    return {**order, "customer_name": customer["name"], "customer_email": customer["email"]}

curl -s -X POST localhost:8031/customers -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Grace Hopper","email":"grace@example.com"}'
# {"id":1,"name":"Grace Hopper","email":"grace@example.com"}

curl -s -X POST localhost:8032/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"customer_id":1,"item":"compiler manual","quantity":1}'
# {"id":1,"customer_id":1,"item":"compiler manual","quantity":1}

curl -s localhost:8032/orders/1 -w "\ntime:%{time_total}\n"
# {"id":1,"customer_id":1,"item":"compiler manual","quantity":1,"customer_name":"Grace Hopper","customer_email":"grace@example.com"}
# time:0.011994

The monolith's equivalent call in Lesson 1 measured time_total: 0.000911. This split version measured 0.011994 — roughly 13x slower for the exact same logical operation, entirely because a dict lookup became an HTTP round trip. That cost was predicted in Lesson 1's discussion; here it's measured directly, on the same two pieces of business logic, before and after the split.

docs.title: Two new failure modes that didn't exist in the monolith
docs.text:
curl -s -w "\nHTTP:%{http_code}\n" -X POST localhost:8032/orders \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"customer_id":999,"item":"ghost item","quantity":1}'
# {"detail":"unknown customer_id"}
# HTTP:400

This one is a correct, intentional validation — Orders Service explicitly checks with Customers Service before creating an order, something the monolith got for free from a single shared dict.

pkill -f "uvicorn customers_service:app"

curl -s -w "\nHTTP:%{http_code}\n" localhost:8032/orders/1
# {"detail":"order found, but customers service is unreachable to enrich it"}
# HTTP:503

curl -s -w "\nHTTP:%{http_code}\n" -X POST localhost:8032/orders \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"customer_id":1,"item":"another item","quantity":1}'
# {"detail":"customers service unreachable"}
# HTTP:503

Both of these failure modes are genuinely new. In the monolith, customers could never be "unreachable" relative to orders — they were the same process. Now, Orders Service's ability to create or even just read an order is coupled to Customers Service's availability, exactly as Lesson 1 warned in the abstract. Notice also that the two 503s have different, honest messages — get_order says the order was found but couldn't be enriched, while create_order never got far enough to create anything. That distinction matters: a client seeing the first error knows the order exists; a client seeing the second knows it doesn't.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This project makes concrete every tradeoff discussed across Lessons 1–9: the bounded-context split ( Customer vs Order, Lesson 2) was sized correctly enough that each service has a clear, independent reason to exist (Lesson 3); the communication between them is synchronous REST (Lesson 4, Lesson 5) because create_order genuinely cannot proceed without knowing the customer exists; and the new 503 failure paths are exactly the kind of partial failure that a production system would want wrapped in a circuit breaker (Level 3) rather than left as a raw, immediate error on every single request while Customers Service is down.

What this project does not yet have, and what the next two levels build: no saga or compensation logic if a multi-step operation partially fails (Level 2), no resilience pattern softening the all-or-nothing 503 into a degraded-but-functional response (Level 3), and no story for how Orders Service finds Customers Service other than a hardcoded URL (solved for a single hardcoded case already, but see Lesson 9 for why that doesn't scale).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating "the split works" (requests succeed) as the finish line without also measuring the real cost (the 13x latency increase shown above) — a split that's never actually necessary for this system's real scale or team structure just paid that cost for nothing.
  • Writing the cross-service validation (unknown customer_id) but forgetting the cross-service unavailability case (customers service unreachable) — both httpx.ConnectError and a 404 response are real things orders_service.py had to handle that monolith.py never needed to think about.
  • Giving the two new 503 error paths the same generic message, which would recreate the exact gateway mistake from Lesson 7 — this project's two distinct, honest error messages are intentional.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a third endpoint to orders_service.py, GET /orders/{oid}/summary, that returns just {"item": ..., "quantity": ...} with no call to Customers Service at all. Confirm with curl -w "time:%{time_total}\n" that this endpoint's latency is close to the original monolith's ~1ms, not the ~12ms of the enriched /orders/{oid} endpoint — proving that the 13x cost measured above is specifically the price of that one join, not an inherent property of Orders Service as a whole.

docs.title: Level 2 · Data & Consistency Across Services
docs.text:
Level 2 is where microservices stop being a networking exercise and become a data-modeling one. Once each service owns its own data, you lose the one thing a monolith gave you for free: a single transaction that touches everything. This level shows, with a real database-backed saga, exactly what you do instead.

What was run, and what wasn't

This level runs two real services, each with its own real SQLite database, coordinated through a real saga orchestrator service and a real outbox table polled on an interval. Every piece of output shown — including a deliberately failed step and its compensating transaction — is real, observed output. A full enterprise event bus (Kafka, RabbitMQ) is intentionally not required here; see the Kafka Mastery Path for that layer in depth.

Prerequisites: Level 1, plus basic SQL comfort.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Database-per-Service & Why Shared Databases Break Down: the coupling a shared schema creates, shown with a real migration that breaks a second service.
  2. Data Ownership & Avoiding Distributed Joins: who's allowed to write what, and how reads work without a join across services.
  3. Propagating Data: Sync Lookups vs Async Events: keeping a local read-optimized copy versus calling out every time.
  4. The Saga Pattern: Orchestration vs Choreography: two working implementations of the same multi-step transaction.
  5. The Outbox Pattern Without Kafka: a real polling-based outbox that survives a crash between the write and the publish.
  6. Idempotency at the Application Layer: making a retried request safe, demonstrated by firing the same request twice on purpose.
  7. CQRS Across Service Boundaries: separate read and write models, and why they drift on purpose.
  8. Handling Partial Failures & Eventual Consistency: what a user actually sees during the inconsistency window, measured, not assumed.
  9. Testing Data Consistency Across Services: writing a test that actually catches a broken saga.
  10. Project: A Real Saga With a Real Compensating Transaction: an order-and-payment saga where the payment step is made to fail, on purpose, and the order gets rolled back for real.

docs.title: After Level 2
docs.text: Level 3 assumes services will fail — not might, will — and builds the resilience patterns (circuit breakers, bulkheads, service mesh) that keep one failing service from taking down everything that calls it.

docs.title: Database-per-Service & Why Shared Databases Break Down
What was run
docs.text: A real SQLite database, shared_shop.db, read directly by two independent scripts standing in for two services. One script (orders_reads_shared.py) represents Orders Service reading a customers table it doesn't own. A real migration was then applied directly against that same file — standing in for Customers Service deploying independently — and the Orders Service script was re-run against the now-changed schema with no code changes of its own.

docs.title: Before the migration, it works
docs.text:
# orders_reads_shared.py — Orders Service, reading a table it doesn't own, directly
row = conn.execute("SELECT id, name, email FROM customers WHERE id = 1").fetchone()

python3 orders_reads_shared.py
# Orders Service read customer: id=1 name=Ada Lovelace email=ada@example.com

docs.title: Customers Service ships an unrelated, reasonable migration
docs.text:
ALTER TABLE customers DROP COLUMN email;
ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN contact_info TEXT;  -- a JSON blob, to support phone + email + preferences later

This is, from Customers Service's point of view, an entirely internal, reasonable refactor: replacing one scalar column with a more flexible structure, something any team should be free to do without asking permission.

python3 orders_reads_shared.py
# Orders Service query FAILED: no such column: email

That's a real sqlite3.OperationalError, not a simulated one. Orders Service didn't change a single line of its own code. It broke because it depended directly on Customers Service's internal table structure — a dependency that was invisible until the moment it broke in production.

docs.title: The fix: each service owns its own database, period
docs.text:
# customers_own_db.py — a real FastAPI service with its own, private SQLite file
conn = sqlite3.connect("customers_only.db")
@app.get("/customers/{cid}")
def get_customer(cid: int):
    row = conn.execute("SELECT id, name, contact_info FROM customers WHERE id = ?", (cid,)).fetchone()
    return {"id": row[0], "name": row[1], "contact_info": row[2]}

curl -s localhost:8041/customers/1
# {"id":1,"name":"Ada Lovelace","contact_info":"{\"email\":\"ada@example.com\"}"}

Now Customers Service can rename, drop, or restructure any column in customers_only.db it wants, as often as it wants, and the only thing any other service can depend on is the shape of the JSON this endpoint returns — a contract Customers Service controls and can version deliberately, the way Lesson 5 of Level 1 covered. No other process even has a file handle open on customers_only.db.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A shared database creates a dependency that bypasses every service boundary built in Level 1: it doesn't matter how cleanly you drew the line between Orders and Customers in your API design if both processes also read and write the same tables directly, because the real contract between them becomes the full SQL schema — every column, every type, every constraint — not the deliberately small, versioned API either team intended to expose. This is why the error above says "no such column," not "API contract violation": the dependency was never going through anything that could enforce or version a contract in the first place.

Database-per-service means each service's data lives in storage only that service's code can access directly. Every other service that needs that data must go through the owning service's API (synchronously, as a REST/gRPC call, or asynchronously, as an event) — never a direct connection to its tables. This gives a service real freedom to change its internal schema whenever it wants, as long as its public API contract stays stable (or is versioned deliberately when it can't). The real cost, covered across the rest of this level, is that this removes the one thing a shared database gave you for free: a single ACID transaction spanning both services' data. Lessons 4 and 5 build the saga and outbox patterns that replace that lost atomicity.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Sharing one database "temporarily, just for this one urgent feature" — the coupling this creates is invisible until the exact moment shown above, and by then it's load-bearing production behavior, not a quick fix to revert.
  • Giving a second service read-only access to the first service's tables, thinking read-only avoids the coupling — it doesn't; the schema dependency and the breakage shown above are identical whether the second service writes or only reads.
  • Splitting services at the API layer while leaving their databases merged "to migrate the data later" — this is a distributed monolith in exactly the sense covered in Level 4, Lesson 8: two deployables, one database-level coupling.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Reproduce this yourself: run setup_shared_db.py, confirm orders_reads_shared.py succeeds, then apply the DROP COLUMN / ADD COLUMN migration shown above and re-run it to see the real failure. Then write a second script, orders_reads_via_api.py, that gets the same customer data by calling http://localhost:8041/customers/1 instead of touching SQLite directly, and confirm that a hypothetical future migration to Customers Service's internal schema (renaming contact_info again, for instance) would no longer be able to break it, as long as the API response shape stays the same.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real customers_service.py (port 8051) with 20 customers, and a real Python script, n_plus_one_demo.py, that enriches 50 orders with customer names two different ways against that live service: one HTTP call per order (50 calls total), and one batch call for all unique customer IDs needed (1 call). Both timings are real, measured on this machine.

docs.title: The distributed join, measured
docs.text:
def enrich_n_plus_1():
    for o in orders:                                              # 50 orders
        r = c.get(f"{CUSTOMERS_URL}/customers/{o['customer_id']}")  # 50 separate HTTP calls
        result.append({**o, "customer_name": r.json()["name"]})

python3 n_plus_one_demo.py
# N+1 (50 separate calls for 50 orders): 0.0574s
# Batched (1 call for 20 unique customers): 0.0101s
# Speedup: 5.7x

Fifty orders referencing only 20 distinct customers means 30 of those 50 calls were redundant — the exact same customer fetched multiple times across different orders. This is the distributed-systems version of the classic "N+1 query" problem familiar from ORMs, except each redundant lookup here is a full network round trip, not a cheap local query.

docs.title: The fix Customers Service had to provide
docs.text:
@app.post("/customers/batch")
def get_customers_batch(ids: list[int]):
    return [customers[i] for i in ids if i in customers]

def enrich_batched():
    ids = sorted({o["customer_id"] for o in orders})              # 20 unique IDs
    r = c.post(f"{CUSTOMERS_URL}/customers/batch", json=ids)       # 1 HTTP call
    by_id = {cust["id"]: cust for cust in r.json()}
    return [{**o, "customer_name": by_id[o["customer_id"]]["name"]} for o in orders]

Critically, Orders Service cannot fix this problem by itself. It can batch its own outgoing requests all it wants, but without a /customers/batch endpoint on the other side, there's no single call to make. The fix required Customers Service — the owner of that data — to decide how bulk access to its own data should work. This is the core idea of data ownership: only the owning service gets to decide the efficient ways to access its data, because only it understands its own storage, indexing, and caching.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
In a monolith, "give me these 20 customers" is one SQL query with a WHERE id IN (...) clause, regardless of how many records the caller happens to need — the database engine already solves this problem. Across a service boundary, every distinct access pattern a consumer needs (single lookup, batch lookup, "all customers updated since timestamp X" for a sync job, etc.) has to be deliberately built as its own endpoint by the owning service, because an owning service's whole point is to not expose its internal storage directly (the shared-database anti-pattern from Lesson 1).

This creates a real, ongoing API design responsibility for the owning service that a monolith's shared database never demanded: anticipate the real access patterns consumers need, and expose them explicitly — a batch endpoint, a pagination scheme, a "changed since" endpoint for sync — rather than forcing every consumer to either hammer it with N+1 calls (as measured above) or reach around it into its database (as Lesson 1 showed breaking). The data owner, not the data consumer, carries this responsibility, because only the owner can change its efficient-access strategy (add an index, add a cache) without needing every consumer to change too.

The alternative some systems reach for — giving each consumer a local, denormalized copy of the data it needs, updated asynchronously via events — avoids the N+1 problem differently by not calling the owning service per-request at all. That's the CQRS pattern covered in Lesson 7, and it trades the network cost measured here for a staleness cost instead.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Blaming the consuming service for "too many calls" when the real fix (a batch endpoint) can only be built by the owning service — data ownership means the fix for bad data-access ergonomics is the owner's job, not the consumer's workaround.
  • Building a batch endpoint with no upper limit on how many IDs can be requested at once, turning a fix for N+1 into a new way to send one enormous, slow request instead.
  • Exposing a generic query/filter endpoint ("send me any SQL-like filter") instead of a small number of deliberate, well-understood access patterns — this reintroduces the shared-database problem one layer up, because now any internal detail a filter can touch is effectively part of the public contract.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a limit to /customers/batch (reject requests for more than, say, 100 IDs with a 400), then modify n_plus_one_demo.py to generate 150 orders referencing 120 unique customers and confirm the batch call now correctly fails with your new limit. Write down one real pagination or chunking strategy you'd use to still serve that request efficiently without removing the limit.

docs.title: Propagating Data: Sync Lookups vs Async Events
What was run
docs.text: A real customers_service.py (port 8061) and a real orders_with_local_cache.py (port 8062) that maintains an in-memory local copy of one customer record, refreshed by a background thread every 3 seconds. The customer's name was changed live, and both a cached read and a live read were taken immediately afterward, then the cached read was taken again after waiting past the refresh interval.

docs.title: Two ways to read the same data, and the real gap between them
docs.text:
# Cached path: zero network calls on the request path, served from local memory
@app.get("/orders/sample-with-cached-name")
def sample_cached():
    cached = local_cache.get(1, {"name": "<not cached yet>"})
    return {"customer_name_from_cache": cached.get("name")}

# Live path: one network call to Customers Service, every single request
@app.get("/orders/sample-with-live-lookup")
def sample_live():
    r = httpx.get(f"{CUSTOMERS_URL}/customers/1", timeout=2.0)
    return {"customer_name_live": r.json()["name"]}

curl -s -X PUT localhost:8061/customers/1/name -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"Ada Lovelace-Byron"}'
# {"id":1,"name":"Ada Lovelace-Byron","updated_at":1792950751.01}

# immediately after:
curl -s localhost:8062/orders/sample-with-live-lookup
# {"order_item":"keyboard","customer_name_live":"Ada Lovelace-Byron"}   <- correct immediately

curl -s localhost:8062/orders/sample-with-cached-name
# {"order_item":"keyboard","customer_name_from_cache":"Ada Lovelace"}   <- STALE, the old name

# after waiting 4 seconds (past the 3-second refresh interval):
curl -s localhost:8062/orders/sample-with-cached-name
# {"order_item":"keyboard","customer_name_from_cache":"Ada Lovelace-Byron"}   <- now correct

This is a real, measured staleness window, not a theoretical one: for up to POLL_INTERVAL seconds (3, in this demo) after a real update, the cached read serves data that is simply wrong. The live-lookup path never has this problem — but it also never stops needing Customers Service to be reachable, which is exactly the coupling Lesson 1 of Level 1 measured as a real cost in the opposite direction.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Every time one service needs another service's data, there are really only two strategies, and this lesson's demo makes both concrete:

  • Pull it live, every time (the sample-with-live-lookup path): always correct as of the moment of the call, at the cost of a network round trip on every single request and a hard availability coupling to the data owner.
  • Keep a local copy, propagated some other way (the sample-with-cached-name path): no network call on the request path, no availability coupling — but the local copy is, by construction, always at risk of being stale by however long it's been since the last successful propagation.

This demo propagates by polling on an interval, which is simple but wasteful (most polls find nothing changed) and caps the staleness window at the poll interval, no tighter. The two more scalable alternatives, both of which trade polling's waste for more infrastructure:

  • Event-driven propagation: the owning service publishes an event the moment something actually changes ("customer 1's name changed"), and consumers update their local copy only when an event arrives — the staleness window becomes "however long event delivery takes," typically milliseconds, not a fixed poll interval. This is the natural next step once you have a real message broker, covered in depth in the Kafka Mastery Path.
  • Change-data-capture: tailing the owning service's database transaction log directly to produce the same kind of change events, without the owning service's application code needing to publish anything itself.

The deciding question, mirroring Level 1's sync/async lesson: can this read tolerate being stale, and if so, by how much? A dashboard showing yesterday's sales totals can tolerate a lot of staleness. A page showing whether an item is currently in stock, right before checkout, usually cannot — that calls for the live path, or an event-driven propagation path with a staleness window measured in milliseconds, not seconds.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Choosing a cache without ever stating, out loud, how stale is acceptable — "it's cached" with no bound on staleness is a silent correctness risk, not a performance optimization.
  • Polling on a fixed interval when most polls find nothing changed, wasting both the network call and the owning service's capacity for no benefit — this is exactly what event-driven propagation is designed to fix.
  • Forgetting that a local cache needs an answer for "what if this value was never cached yet" (the "<not cached yet>" fallback above) — a cache's cold-start behavior is as much a design decision as its refresh strategy.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Change POLL_INTERVAL to 1 second, repeat the name-update experiment, and measure the real staleness window with timestamps printed on both sides (when the PUT was sent, when the cached value actually changed). Then write down, for a feature you're familiar with (from this course or elsewhere), whether a 1-second staleness window would be acceptable for it, and why.

docs.title: The Saga Pattern: Orchestration vs Choreography
What was run
docs.text: Four real services: order_service.py (8071), payment_service.py (8072, which really declines payments over $1000), inventory_service.py (8073, which really rejects one specific item as out of stock), and orchestrator.py (8070) coordinating all three. Three real checkouts were run: one that succeeds completely, one that fails at the payment step, and one that fails at the inventory step after payment already succeeded — exercising a real multi-step compensation.

docs.title: A saga that completes
docs.text:
curl -s -X POST localhost:8070/checkout -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"item":"laptop","amount_cents":50000}'
# {"saga":"COMPLETED","order":{"id":1,"item":"laptop","amount_cents":50000,"status":"CONFIRMED"},
#  "payment":{"id":1,"order_id":1,"amount_cents":50000,"status":"CHARGED"},
#  "reservation":{"id":1,"order_id":1,"item":"laptop","status":"RESERVED"}}

Three real services, three real state changes, one logical transaction with no shared database underneath it.

docs.title: Failure at step 2: one compensation
docs.text:
curl -s -X POST localhost:8070/checkout -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"item":"yacht","amount_cents":500000}'
# {"saga":"FAILED","failed_step":"payment",
#  "reason":"payment declined: amount_cents 500000 exceeds fraud limit 100000",
#  "compensations_run":["order_cancelled"],
#  "order":{"id":2,"item":"yacht","amount_cents":500000,"status":"CANCELLED"}}

pay_resp = http.post(f"{PAYMENT_URL}/payments", json={"order_id": order["id"], "amount_cents": c.amount_cents})
if pay_resp.status_code != 200:
    http.post(f"{ORDER_URL}/orders/{order['id']}/cancel")   # undo step 1
    return {"saga": "FAILED", "failed_step": "payment", "compensations_run": ["order_cancelled"], ...}

Order #2 really exists in order_service.py's memory with status CANCELLED, not deleted — the saga's failure is recorded, not erased. No payment record was created at all, confirmed directly: curl -s localhost:8072/payments still shows only payment id: 1 from the first, successful checkout.

docs.title: Failure at step 3: two compensations, in reverse order
docs.text:
curl -s -X POST localhost:8070/checkout -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"item":"discontinued-widget","amount_cents":2000}'
# {"saga":"FAILED","failed_step":"inventory",
#  "reason":"'discontinued-widget' is out of stock",
#  "compensations_run":["payment_refunded","order_cancelled"],
#  "order":{"id":3,"item":"discontinued-widget","amount_cents":2000,"status":"CANCELLED"},
#  "payment":{"id":2,"order_id":3,"amount_cents":2000,"status":"REFUNDED"}}

inv_resp = http.post(f"{INVENTORY_URL}/reservations", json={"order_id": order["id"], "item": c.item})
if inv_resp.status_code != 200:
    http.post(f"{PAYMENT_URL}/payments/{payment['id']}/refund")    # undo step 2
    http.post(f"{ORDER_URL}/orders/{order['id']}/cancel")           # undo step 1, in reverse order
    return {"saga": "FAILED", "failed_step": "inventory", "compensations_run": ["payment_refunded", "order_cancelled"], ...}

By the time inventory rejected discontinued-widget, payment id: 2 had really charged $20.00 against order 3. The orchestrator's compensation logic ran a real POST /payments/2/refund, flipping its status to REFUNDED — a second, separate, real state transition, not a rollback of the first transaction, because there is no shared transaction to roll back.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A saga is a sequence of local transactions, each in a different service, where each step either succeeds and moves to the next step, or fails and triggers compensating transactions that semantically undo every step that already succeeded — in reverse order, as shown above. This is fundamentally different from a database rollback: a compensating transaction is a new, forward-moving operation (REFUNDED, CANCELLED) that happened at a real point in time, not an erasure of history. This matters because other things may have already observed the intermediate state — a dashboard might have already shown "payment charged" for order 3 before the refund ran, and that was true at the time, even though the final state is "refunded."

This demo implements orchestration: one coordinator (orchestrator.py) explicitly calls each step in order and explicitly decides what to compensate on failure. The alternative, choreography, has no central coordinator: each service reacts to events from the previous step and emits its own event when done, with compensation triggered by services reacting to a "step failed" event the same way they reacted to a "step succeeded" one. Concretely, a choreographed version of this saga would have Order Service publish OrderCreated, Payment Service subscribe to it and publish PaymentCharged or PaymentFailed, and Inventory Service subscribe to PaymentCharged — with Order Service also subscribing to PaymentFailed to cancel itself, instead of a coordinator calling cancel directly.

The real tradeoff: orchestration keeps the whole saga's logic in one readable place (as this demo's checkout function shows end-to-end) but creates a coordinator that knows about every participating service. Choreography removes that central coordinator and lets each service stay fully independent, but the saga's actual logic — "what happens when payment fails" — is now scattered across every service's event handlers, with no single place to read the whole flow, which gets genuinely hard to reason about past 3–4 steps.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating the orchestrator's checkout function as if it ran inside one transaction — it does not; a crash between step 2 and step 3 (payment charged, inventory call never made) leaves the system in CHARGED/no reservation until something retries or compensates it, which is exactly the durability gap Level 1, Lesson 4 first exposed and Lesson 5 of this level addresses properly.
  • Writing a compensating transaction that assumes the original action fully succeeded, with no handling for "what if the thing I'm compensating never actually finished" — a refund call to a payment that was never actually charged needs to be a safe no-op, not a crash.
  • Choosing choreography for its decoupling benefits without first making sure every team involved can actually find and read every event handler across every service — the "no central coordinator" benefit becomes a real debugging cost the first time someone has to trace a failed saga across five services' logs instead of one orchestrator's.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Kill the orchestrator.py process with kill -9 between the payment-charge call and the inventory-reservation call (add a time.sleep(10) right there temporarily, and kill it during the sleep). Restart it, and confirm for yourself, by querying /payments and /reservations directly, that order's payment is left CHARGED forever with no reservation and no compensation — because the in-memory orchestrator has no record that this saga was ever in progress. Write one sentence on what persistent state the orchestrator would need to recover and finish (or compensate) that saga after a real restart.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real order_service_outbox.py (port 8081) writing to a real SQLite file, orders_outbox.db, with an orders table and an outbox table written in the same transaction. The service was then killed with kill -9 — a real hard crash, not a graceful shutdown — and the outbox row's survival was confirmed by reading the SQLite file directly with a separate Python process while the service was still dead. A separate outbox_poller.py process and shipping_service.py (port 8082) were started afterward to show the surviving row get delivered automatically.

docs.title: Writing the order and its outbox entry atomically
docs.text:
@app.post("/orders")
def create_order(o: OrderIn):
    cur = conn.cursor()
    cur.execute("INSERT INTO orders (item) VALUES (?)", (o.item,))
    oid = cur.lastrowid
    cur.execute("INSERT INTO outbox (order_id, payload) VALUES (?, ?)", (oid, json.dumps({"order_id": oid, "address": o.address})))
    conn.commit()   # both rows commit together, or neither does

curl -s -X POST localhost:8081/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"item":"bookshelf","address":"42 Wallaby Way"}'
# {"id":1,"item":"bookshelf"}

curl -s localhost:8081/outbox
# [{"id":1,"order_id":1,"payload":"{\"order_id\": 1, \"address\": \"42 Wallaby Way\"}","published":false}]

docs.title: A real crash, and the real proof the row survives it
docs.text:
pkill -9 -f "uvicorn order_service_outbox:app"   # a real SIGKILL, no graceful shutdown

python3 -c "
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect('orders_outbox.db')
print(conn.execute('SELECT id, order_id, payload, published FROM outbox').fetchall())
"
# [(1, 1, '{"order_id": 1, "address": "42 Wallaby Way"}', 0)]

The order service process is dead. No Python object holding that outbox row exists anywhere in memory. The row is still there, because SQLite's conn.commit() fsyncs it to disk as part of a real transaction — this is the entire point of the pattern, and it's the thing Level 1, Lesson 4's in-memory queue.Queue fundamentally could not provide: that demo's queued job would have been gone forever after a crash like this one. This one isn't.

docs.title: Recovery, with no special "recovery mode" needed
docs.text:
uvicorn shipping_service:app --port 8082 &      # Shipping comes up
python3 outbox_poller.py &                       # a separate process, polling the same SQLite file

# a few seconds later:
curl -s localhost:8082/shipments
# [{"order_id":1,"address":"42 Wallaby Way"}]

python3 -c "... SELECT published FROM outbox ..."
# [(1, 1, '...', 1)]   <- published flipped to 1

Nothing about the poller's logic knows or cares that the order service crashed in between. It just scans for published = 0 rows, same as it always does — crash recovery here isn't a special code path, it's the absence of a special code path, because the durable state (the SQLite file) never depended on any one process staying alive.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The core problem the outbox pattern solves is the "dual write" problem: a service needs to both change its own state (create the order) and reliably notify another system about it (tell Shipping), and those two things cannot be one atomic operation if the notification is a network call to a different service — exactly the gap Level 1, Lesson 4 demonstrated with its fragile in-memory queue. The outbox pattern turns this into a single-database problem instead: write the state change and a durable record of "this needs to be sent" in the same local transaction, which the database already knows how to make atomic. A separate process (the poller here; in production, often a tool like Debezium reading the database's write-ahead log instead of polling a table directly) is then responsible for reliably getting that durable record out to wherever it needs to go, retrying as needed, with no risk of losing it because it only ever reads already-committed state.

This demo's time.sleep(2) polling loop is the simplest possible version of "a separate process delivers outbox rows" and has a real, honest limitation: it adds up to 2 seconds of latency between an order being created and its shipment request being sent, and it does real wasted work scanning for rows even when there's nothing new. A message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ) removes that polling delay by having the poller push to a topic the moment it finds a new row, and lets consumers subscribe instead of the producer needing to know every downstream consumer's URL directly, as this demo's poller does.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Writing the business-state change and the outbox row in two separate transactions (even to the same database) — this reintroduces exactly the dual-write race the pattern exists to close; they must be one transaction.
  • Deleting outbox rows after publishing instead of marking them published — losing the row removes your own audit trail of what was sent and when, which matters the first time you need to debug "did this shipment request ever actually get sent?"
  • Running more than one poller instance against the same table with no locking — two pollers can both pick up the same unpublished row and send it twice, which is why real implementations add a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED or equivalent claim step before publishing.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Modify outbox_poller.py to also record a delivery_attempts count and a last_error column on the outbox table, incrementing it on every failed send. Stop shipping_service.py, create two new orders, let the poller retry for about 10 seconds, then restart Shipping and confirm both orders are eventually delivered and delivery_attempts shows a real count greater than zero for both.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real payment_service.py (port 8091) with two endpoints against the exact same business operation: a naive one with no protection, and one that checks an Idempotency-Key header before charging. Both were called multiple times with curl, simulating a client that retries a request after not receiving a response — a real, common failure mode whenever a network call times out and the client can't tell whether the server actually processed it before the timeout.

docs.title: The naive endpoint, retried, charges twice for real
docs.text:
@app.post("/charges-naive")
def charge_naive(c: ChargeIn):
    cid = next(seq)
    charges.append({"id": cid, "amount_cents": c.amount_cents})
    return {"id": cid, "amount_cents": c.amount_cents}

curl -s -X POST localhost:8091/charges-naive -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"amount_cents":5000}'
# {"id":1,"amount_cents":5000}
curl -s -X POST localhost:8091/charges-naive -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"amount_cents":5000}'
# {"id":2,"amount_cents":5000}

curl -s localhost:8091/charges-naive/all
# [{"id":1,"amount_cents":5000},{"id":2,"amount_cents":5000}]

Two real charge records, id: 1 and id: 2, for what was meant to be one $50.00 charge. In a real payment system, this is a customer getting billed twice because their client (or a retry layer, or a flaky mobile network) sent the same logical request more than once — exactly the scenario Level 1, Lesson 4's async retry loop would create if it ever retried a non-idempotent call.

docs.title: The idempotent endpoint, retried, charges exactly once
docs.text:
@app.post("/charges-idempotent")
def charge_idempotent(c: ChargeIn, idempotency_key: str = Header(...)):
    if idempotency_key in idempotency_store:
        return {**idempotency_store[idempotency_key], "replayed": True}   # same result, no new charge
    cid = next(seq)
    result = {"id": cid, "amount_cents": c.amount_cents, "replayed": False}
    idempotency_store[idempotency_key] = result
    return result

curl -s -X POST localhost:8091/charges-idempotent -H 'Idempotency-Key: req-abc-123' -d '{"amount_cents":5000}'
# {"id":3,"amount_cents":5000,"replayed":false}
curl -s -X POST localhost:8091/charges-idempotent -H 'Idempotency-Key: req-abc-123' -d '{"amount_cents":5000}'
# {"id":3,"amount_cents":5000,"replayed":true}
curl -s -X POST localhost:8091/charges-idempotent -H 'Idempotency-Key: req-abc-123' -d '{"amount_cents":5000}'
# {"id":3,"amount_cents":5000,"replayed":true}

curl -s localhost:8091/charges-idempotent/all
# [{"id":3,"amount_cents":5000,"replayed":false}]

Three real HTTP requests, the same Idempotency-Key on all three, and exactly one real charge record (id: 3) in the final list. The second and third calls returned the same id: 3 with "replayed": true, telling the caller plainly that nothing new happened — they got back the original result, not a fresh charge.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
An idempotent operation is one that produces the same effect no matter how many times it's performed with the same input. GET and DELETE are naturally idempotent (reading twice doesn't change anything; deleting an already-deleted thing is a no-op). POST — "create a new charge" — is inherently not idempotent by default, because its whole point is to create something new each time, which is exactly the naive endpoint's problem above.

The idempotency key pattern fixes this at the application layer by having the caller generate a unique key per logical operation (a UUID generated once, before the first attempt) and send it on every retry of that same logical operation. The server's job is then to remember, for each key, the result it already returned, and return that same result again — without re-running the side-effecting logic — for any repeat of that key. This requires the key store itself to be durable across the same kind of crash discussed in Lesson 5: this demo's in-memory idempotency_store dict would lose every key on a restart, which would make every pending retry look brand-new again — a real production implementation stores idempotency keys in the same durable database as the charges themselves, ideally checked and written in the same transaction as the charge.

This is a necessary complement to the saga pattern from Lesson 4: a saga step that calls Payment Service might itself be retried (by the orchestrator, after a timeout it couldn't distinguish from a real failure) — without idempotency protection on that call, a saga retry could double-charge a customer even though the saga's own logic was working exactly as designed.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Generating a new idempotency key on every retry instead of reusing the same one generated at the start of the logical operation — this defeats the entire mechanism, since the server has no way to recognize a retry from a genuinely new request.
  • Keying the idempotency store only by a short-lived in-memory structure (as this demo deliberately does, to keep the example small) — a real implementation needs the key store to survive a restart, or every pending retry after a deploy becomes a fresh, unprotected charge.
  • Treating idempotency keys as a replacement for distinguishing genuinely different requests with the same parameters — two real, separate $50 charges by the same customer on the same day need two different keys; the key identifies the request attempt, not the payment amount.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a check to charge_idempotent that returns a real 409 Conflict if the same Idempotency-Key is reused with a different amount_cents than the first time it was seen — this catches a real bug class (a client reusing a key across genuinely different logical operations) that the current implementation silently ignores by just replaying the original amount. Test it with curl using the same key twice but a different amount the second time, and confirm you get a real 409, not a silently wrong replayed result.

docs.title: The query, two ways, timed
docs.text:
# write_service.py — correct, but must aggregate over every matching row, every time
@app.get("/customers/{cid}/total-spent-computed-live")
def total_spent_live(cid: int):
    row = conn.execute("SELECT SUM(amount_cents), COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?", (cid,)).fetchone()
    return {"customer_id": cid, "total_cents": row[0] or 0, "order_count": row[1]}

# read_service.py — pre-computed by a separate projector process, always a single-row lookup
@app.get("/customers/{cid}/total-spent-from-read-model")
def total_spent_read_model(cid: int):
    row = conn.execute("SELECT total_cents, order_count FROM customer_totals WHERE customer_id = ?", (cid,)).fetchone()
    return {"customer_id": cid, "total_cents": row[0], "order_count": row[1]}

# warmed-up timings, orders table at 300,500 rows:
curl -s localhost:8102/customers/1/total-spent-from-read-model -o /dev/null -w "time:%{time_total}\n"
# time:0.000868   (and 0.001005, 0.002058 across repeats)

curl -s localhost:8101/customers/1/total-spent-computed-live -o /dev/null -w "time:%{time_total}\n"
# time:0.006638   (and 0.007020, 0.007635 across repeats)

The read model answered in roughly a quarter to an eighth of the time of the live aggregate, consistently, because it's a primary-key lookup against a tiny pre-aggregated table instead of a scan-and-sum over every order row.

docs.title: The real bug this setup exposed, honestly
docs.text:
curl -s localhost:8102/customers/1/total-spent-from-read-model
# {"customer_id":1,"total_cents":500000,"order_count":500}

curl -s localhost:8101/customers/1/total-spent-computed-live
# {"customer_id":1,"total_cents":650000,"order_count":650}

These two numbers disagree, and not because of ordinary eventual-consistency lag — the read model is correctly showing the 500 orders that went through create_order() and its outbox row. The 300,000 bulk rows were inserted directly into the orders table with a raw INSERT that never touched the outbox table, so the projector never saw them and never updated customer_totals for the ~150 of those rows that happened to belong to customer 1. The read model isn't being slow to catch up — it's permanently missing data that bypassed its only input pipeline. This is a completely real, common CQRS failure mode, not a contrived one: any write path that doesn't go through the same event/outbox mechanism the projector depends on will silently drift the read model and never self-correct.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) separates the model used to write data (the command side — write_service.py's normalized orders table, optimized for correctly recording individual transactions) from the model used to read data (the query side — read_model.db's denormalized customer_totals table, optimized for answering one specific question fast). The two models don't have to use the same schema, the same database technology, or even the same service — the read side can be a completely different service, scaled and optimized independently of the write side, exactly as this demo splits them.

The connective tissue between the two sides — here, the outbox + projector from Lesson 5 — is doing real, critical work: it's the only path by which the write side's changes reach the read side. This lesson's bug demonstrates the sharp edge of that design directly: a read model is only as complete as its event pipeline's coverage of every possible write path. A system that has even one write path skipping the outbox (a backfill script, an admin tool, a different service writing directly to the same table) will have a read model that's wrong in a way that never fixes itself, no matter how long you wait — unlike ordinary replication lag, which resolves on its own given time.

This is the deeper reason CQRS is usually paired with event sourcing or at least a single, disciplined write path: if the write model's only way of mutating state already goes through an event that the read side also consumes, there's no way to "bypass" the pipeline, because there's no other way to write at all.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a CQRS read-model discrepancy as "it'll catch up eventually" without first checking whether every write path actually produces an event — as shown above, some discrepancies are permanent, not transient lag.
  • Letting a second write path (an admin panel, a migration script, direct database access for "just this once") write to the command side's tables without going through the same code path that produces outbox events.
  • Building a read model as a premature optimization before measuring whether the live-aggregate query is actually too slow for its real use case — Lesson 2's data-ownership lesson applies here too: build the access pattern the consumer actually needs, when it's actually needed.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Write a small reconciliation script that compares, for every customer with at least one order, the write side's live-computed total against the read model's stored total, and prints every customer where they disagree. Run it against this demo's data and confirm it surfaces the discrepancy found above. Then fix the root cause: modify the bulk-insert step to also write corresponding outbox rows, re-run the projector, and confirm the reconciliation script reports zero discrepancies afterward.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: The real saga from Lesson 4 — order_service.py, payment_service.py, inventory_service.py, orchestrator.py — with a real time.sleep(2.5) added to payment_service.py's /payments endpoint, standing in for a real card-network round trip that isn't instant. A real Python script then started a checkout in a background thread and polled the order's status directly, with real timestamps, while the saga was still running.

docs.title: The inconsistency window, measured with real timestamps
docs.text:
t.start()                                      # kicks off POST /checkout in a background thread
time.sleep(0.3)
r = httpx.get(f'http://localhost:8071/orders/{last_oid}')
print(f"[t+{time.time()-t0:.2f}s] status while saga in flight: {r.json()['status']}")

tracking order id 6
[t+0.52s] status while saga in flight: PENDING
[t+2.06s] status while saga in flight: PENDING
[t+2.56s] saga finished: COMPLETED
[t+2.58s] final status: CONFIRMED

For a real, measured 2.56 seconds, any client that looked up order 6 — a status page, a mobile app polling for confirmation, a different service checking whether it's safe to proceed — would have seen PENDING, a status that is truthful (the order genuinely isn't confirmed yet) but incomplete (the order is, in fact, in the middle of successfully completing, not stuck or failed). Only after the full saga finished did the status flip to CONFIRMED.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A monolith processing this same checkout inside one database transaction would show the client either "order doesn't exist yet" or "order exists and is fully confirmed" — there's no observable in-between state, because the whole operation is atomic from any outside observer's point of view. A saga, by construction, cannot offer that: it is a sequence of independently committing local transactions, so there necessarily exists a real window, after step 1 commits and before the last step commits, where the system's state is genuinely partial — true at that instant, but not the final answer.

This is what "eventual consistency" concretely means: the system will reach a consistent, correct final state (CONFIRMED or CANCELLED, never stuck forever assuming the saga completes or is properly compensated), but not instantly, and any reader during the window in between sees a real, valid, but temporary state. The practical questions this raises, all of which need an explicit answer rather than an accidental one:

  • What should the client do with a PENDING status? Often: show a "processing" state, not an error, and poll or subscribe for the final result rather than treating PENDING as a failure.
  • What should a different service do if it reads PENDING mid-saga? If Shipping checked order 6's status during that window to decide whether to prepare a shipment, it needs to know PENDING means "don't act yet," not "this order failed" — the states a saga can be in, and what's safe to do in each, need to be part of the contract other services design against.
  • How long is the window allowed to be? 2.56 seconds here came from one slow payment call; a saga with more steps, or a slower step, has a proportionally longer window — worth measuring deliberately, not discovering in production.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating PENDING (or any intermediate state) as an error case in client code, causing a user to see a failure message for an operation that's actually still succeeding, just not finished yet.
  • Letting a different service make an irreversible decision based on a mid-saga intermediate state without understanding that the state might still change — e.g., reserving a shipping slot for an order that might still be compensated into CANCELLED a moment later.
  • Assuming the inconsistency window is always short enough not to matter — measure it, as this lesson did, rather than guessing; a saga calling a genuinely slow external system (a real payment processor, not a 2.5-second simulation) can have a window measured in many seconds, not fractions of one.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a fourth, intermediate status to order_service.py — AWAITING_PAYMENT — and have the orchestrator set it right after creating the order but before calling Payment Service, instead of leaving the status at the generic PENDING for the whole saga. Repeat this lesson's timed polling experiment and confirm you can now distinguish, from the outside, "waiting on payment" from "waiting on inventory" during the saga's real execution window, not just "something is still pending."

docs.text: A real Python test script, test_saga_consistency.py, calling the live saga from Lesson 4 over real HTTP and asserting a cross-service invariant: if the saga fails at the inventory step, the payment it already charged must end up REFUNDED, not left CHARGED. It was run twice: once against the correct orchestrator.py, and once against a deliberately broken copy, orchestrator_buggy.py, with the refund compensation call removed.

docs.title: The invariant that matters, stated as a real assertion
docs.text:
def test_out_of_stock_item_refunds_the_payment():
    r = httpx.post(f"{ORCHESTRATOR}/checkout", json={"item": "discontinued-widget", "amount_cents": 1500}, timeout=10)
    body = r.json()
    assert body["saga"] == "FAILED"
    assert body["failed_step"] == "inventory"

    latest = [p for p in httpx.get(f"{PAYMENT}/payments").json() if p["amount_cents"] == 1500][-1]
    assert latest["status"] == "REFUNDED", (
        f"consistency violation: payment {latest['id']} is '{latest['status']}', "

    )

python3 test_saga_consistency.py
# PASS: test_successful_checkout_confirms_order
# PASS: test_out_of_stock_item_refunds_the_payment

docs.title: A one-line regression, and the test that actually catches it
docs.text:
# orchestrator_buggy.py -- a "simplification" that deletes the refund call
inv_resp = http.post(f"{INVENTORY_URL}/reservations", json={"order_id": order["id"], "item": c.item})
if inv_resp.status_code != 200:
    http.post(f"{ORDER_URL}/orders/{order['id']}/cancel")   # <- refund call silently missing here
    return {"saga": "FAILED", "failed_step": "inventory", ...}

curl -s -X POST localhost:8075/checkout -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"item":"discontinued-widget","amount_cents":1800}'
# {"saga":"FAILED","failed_step":"inventory",
#  "order":{"id":9,"item":"discontinued-widget","amount_cents":1800,"status":"CANCELLED"},
#  "payment":{"id":6,"order_id":9,"amount_cents":1800,"status":"CHARGED"}}

The order correctly shows CANCELLED — that part of the compensation still runs. The payment, real money charged in this simulation, is left CHARGED forever. Running the same consistency test against this buggy version:

python3 test_saga_consistency_buggy.py
# AssertionError: consistency violation: payment 7 is 'CHARGED', but the saga it belongs to
# FAILED at the inventory step -- it should have been refunded

A real AssertionError, on a real bug, caught by a test that calls real running services over real HTTP — not a unit test of any single service's internal logic, because no single service's internal logic is wrong here. Payment Service correctly charges when asked, correctly refunds when asked; Order Service correctly cancels when asked. The bug is entirely in the interaction — the orchestrator forgetting to ask for a refund — which is precisely the class of bug that disappears from view if you only ever test services in isolation.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Unit tests, run against one service in isolation (often with its dependencies mocked), can tell you a service does what it claims given a specific input. They cannot tell you whether the system of services, working together, upholds a cross-service invariant — "a cancelled order never leaves a charged payment behind" is a property of the whole saga, not of any one service's code. Testing this requires either:

  • A real integration test, as built here: start the real services (or realistic stand-ins), drive them through a real scenario over the network, and assert on the combined resulting state across services — exactly what this lesson's test does.
  • Consumer-driven contract tests (covered in Level 3, Lesson 9), which catch a different but related class of problem: one service breaking another's expectations of its API, without needing every service running at once.

The specific pattern worth generalizing from this test: identify the saga's failure-path invariants — not just "the happy path works," but "every compensation that should run for every real failure mode, actually runs" — and write one assertion per invariant, checked against real post-failure state in every service that participated. Lesson 4's saga has two failure paths (payment declined, inventory out of stock); a thorough test suite needs an invariant check for each, not just the happy path shown as test_successful_checkout_confirms_order above.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Testing only the saga's happy path and never deliberately forcing each failure branch — the bug caught above lives entirely inside a failure branch that a happy-path-only test suite would never execute.
  • Asserting only on the orchestrator's immediate HTTP response ("saga": "FAILED") without also checking the actual downstream state in each participating service — the buggy orchestrator's response here doesn't even mention the payment at all in some code paths, so a test that only reads the orchestrator's reply could easily miss this.
  • Running this kind of test against shared, stateful services without resetting state between runs — this demo's services accumulate orders and payments across test runs (note the real IDs climbing: payment 6, payment 7), which is fine for a quick manual check but would need a reset or unique-per-test identifiers in a real CI suite.

Then introduce a different deliberate bug — have the buggy orchestrator reserve inventory before checking the payment response — and confirm your new test catches that ordering bug too.

What was run

docs.title: The saga, run once, for real
docs.text:

  -d '{"item":"mechanical keyboard","amount_cents":9000}'
# {"saga":"COMPLETED","replayed":false,
#  "order":{"id":11,"item":"mechanical keyboard","amount_cents":9000,"status":"CONFIRMED"},

if existing:

docs.title: Retried, then the process is really killed, then retried again
docs.text:
curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/checkout -H 'Idempotency-Key: ckt-001' -d '{...same body...}'
# {"saga":"COMPLETED","replayed":true, ...same order/payment/reservation ids as before...}

pkill -9 -f "uvicorn orchestrator_durable:app"     # a real, hard crash
uvicorn orchestrator_durable:app --port 8080 &      # a fresh process, fresh memory, nothing cached in RAM

curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/checkout -H 'Idempotency-Key: ckt-001' -d '{...same body...}'
# {"saga":"COMPLETED","replayed":true, ...identical order id 11, payment id 8, reservation id 4...}

curl -s localhost:8072/payments
# [...,{"id":8,"order_id":11,"amount_cents":9000,"status":"CHARGED"}]   <- exactly one payment, id 8

Three real checkout requests with the same Idempotency-Key, spanning a real process crash in between, produced exactly one real order, one real payment, and one real inventory reservation — confirmed directly against payment_service.py's own records, not just trusted from the orchestrator's response. The crash in the middle changed nothing, because the fact "this idempotency key already has a result" lives in saga_log.db on disk, not in the orchestrator process's memory.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This project directly closes the gap that Lesson 4's own exercise raised: an orchestrator that only tracks saga progress in memory loses all of it on a crash, leaving no record that a saga was ever in flight. This version fixes the retry half of that problem — a client that doesn't know whether its request made it through (because the orchestrator crashed, or the network dropped the response) can safely retry with the same key and get the real, authoritative final answer, without risking a duplicate charge, exactly the property Lesson 6 built in isolation and this project now applies to an entire multi-step saga, not just one endpoint.

What this project does not yet fully solve, and what's worth being honest about: it only persists the saga's final result, not its in-progress state. If the orchestrator crashes mid-saga — after charging payment but before reserving inventory — a retry with the same key would find no saga_runs row yet and re-run the entire saga from scratch, potentially double-charging the customer. A fully crash-safe saga needs to persist each step's completion, not just the end result, so a resumed saga can pick up exactly where it left off rather than restarting — the natural next step beyond this project, and close to what dedicated saga/workflow engines (like Temporal or AWS Step Functions) are built specifically to handle.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Persisting only the final saga result (as this project deliberately does, to keep the example reachable) and mistaking that for full crash safety — the honest limitation above (a mid-saga crash can still double-run) is a real gap, not a hypothetical one.
  • Using the idempotency key as the saga's only identifier without also being able to look up a saga by its resulting order ID, payment ID, etc. — in production you'll need both directions of lookup for support and debugging.
  • Never expiring old saga_runs rows — an idempotency log that grows forever is a real, if slow-growing, operational problem; production systems typically expire keys after a bounded window (e.g., 24 hours), long enough to cover realistic retries, short enough not to grow unbounded.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Close the gap named above for real: add a status column to saga_runs (IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETED, FAILED), write a row with IN_PROGRESS immediately after creating the order (before calling Payment), and update it as each step completes. Then simulate a mid-saga crash by adding a time.sleep(10) right after the payment call and killing the process during that sleep. Restart, retry with the same key, and observe what your current implementation does (hint: it will likely re-run everything, since it only checks for a COMPLETED row) — then write, in a comment, what check you'd need to add to detect and safely resume (or safely compensate) an IN_PROGRESS saga instead of blindly re-running it.

docs.title: Level 3 · Resilience & Service Mesh
docs.text:
Level 3 is about what happens the moment one service in your system gets slow or stops responding — which, given enough time and enough services, will happen. This level builds and deliberately breaks real failure-isolation mechanisms, then shows how a service mesh moves a lot of that logic out of application code entirely.

What was run, and what wasn't

This level runs real services with a real circuit breaker library, real injected latency and real killed processes to trigger failures, and a real lightweight sidecar proxy (Envoy, run standalone) to demonstrate the mesh pattern and mTLS. A full production mesh control plane (Istio/Linkerd's control plane, multi-cluster mesh) was not run as part of this course; where that's the case, it's stated plainly and the underlying mechanism is shown with the standalone proxy instead.

Prerequisites: Levels 1–2.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Circuit Breakers: Real Failure Isolation: tripping a real breaker against a real failing dependency, and watching it half-open.
  2. Retries, Timeouts & Backoff Done Right: a real retry storm, caused on purpose, and the jittered backoff that fixes it.
  3. Bulkheads & Resource Isolation: isolating one slow dependency's connection pool so it can't starve the rest of the service.
  4. Rate Limiting Between Services: a real token-bucket limiter protecting a downstream service from a real burst.
  5. Service Mesh Fundamentals: The Sidecar Pattern: a real standalone Envoy proxy sitting in front of a service, with traffic routed through it.
  6. Traffic Management: Canary Releases at the Service Level: splitting real traffic between two versions of a service at the proxy layer.
  7. mTLS & Service-to-Service Security: real self-signed certificates, a real handshake, and what breaks when one side doesn't trust the other's cert.
  8. Distributed Tracing Across Services: a real trace ID propagated across three real service calls, visualized end to end.
  9. Consumer-Driven Contract Testing: a contract test that catches a breaking API change before it ships.
  10. Project: Inject Real Failures and Watch Resilience Work: a small chaos script that kills and slows real services while the system keeps serving most requests.

docs.title: After Level 3
docs.text: Level 4 steps back from any one service to the whole system: how teams are organized around services, how you migrate an existing monolith incrementally instead of in one risky rewrite, and when microservices are the wrong answer.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real flaky_service.py (port 8111) that can be toggled to return real 500s on demand, and a real client using pybreaker (a real, widely-used Python circuit breaker library, not a hand-rolled one) with fail_max=3, reset_timeout=5. The demo script, run_breaker_demo.py, drives the breaker through closed → open → half-open → closed in one run. Every number below was cross-checked against flaky_service's own request log, which is what caught a real, honest surprise in the breaker library's own error reporting.

breaker = pybreaker.CircuitBreaker(fail_max=3, reset_timeout=5)

def call_flaky_service():

--- phase 2: service goes down (real 500s) ---
call 1: real call failed (got 500). breaker_state=closed
call 2: real call failed (got 500). breaker_state=closed
call 3: CIRCUIT OPEN, real call SKIPPED entirely. breaker_state=open
call 4: CIRCUIT OPEN, real call SKIPPED entirely. breaker_state=open
call 5: CIRCUIT OPEN, real call SKIPPED entirely. breaker_state=open

docs.title: The real surprise: checking the service's own log
docs.text:
grep "GET /data" flaky.log
# 200, 200,                          <- phase 1
# 500, 500, 500, 500,                 <- phase 2 + phase 3 combined
# 200, 200                           <- phase 4

That's four real 500s, not the three "real call failed" lines phase 2 printed. Instrumenting the breaker's internal failure counter directly (breaker.fail_counter) resolved it precisely: "call 3," the one printed as "CIRCUIT OPEN, real call SKIPPED entirely," was actually the exact call that tripped the breaker — pybreaker executes the real HTTP request first, and only after that real request fails does it check whether the failure count has now reached fail_max and, if so, re-wrap that same real failure as a CircuitBreakerError instead of the original exception. The fourth real 500 showed up later still: phase 3's "probe call (service still down)" also made a real network request — because reset_timeout (5s) had elapsed by then, pybreaker moved the breaker to half-open and let exactly one real trial call through, which failed for real and was, again, reported as a CircuitBreakerError indistinguishable from a truly skipped call by its exception type alone. Two calls that did reach the network and two different calls that genuinely did not all produce the identical pybreaker.CircuitBreakerError from the caller's point of view.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency with a state machine: closed (calls go through normally; failures are counted), open (calls are rejected immediately, with no network request, once failures cross a threshold), and half-open (after a cooldown, exactly one real trial call is let through to test whether the dependency has recovered — success closes the breaker again, failure reopens it). This demo exercised all three states for real.

The genuinely important lesson from the discrepancy above isn't about pybreaker specifically — it's that a library's own exception type is not always sufficient to tell you whether a real network call happened. The call that trips the breaker, and the periodic half-open probe, both necessarily make a real call (that's the whole point — the breaker needs real evidence to decide), and a library focused on giving callers one consistent error type (CircuitBreakerError) for "this call did not succeed, for breaker-related reasons" can reasonably choose not to distinguish those two very different situations in the exception alone. If you need to know definitively whether a specific call reached the network, the reliable source of truth is the downstream service's own logs or metrics — exactly how this discrepancy was actually caught here — not inference from the client-side exception type.

This matters practically: if you're debugging "why does my dependency's request count not match my circuit breaker's open/closed transitions," the answer is often exactly this — trip calls and half-open probes are real calls wearing the same exception label as a fully-skipped one.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming every CircuitBreakerError (or equivalent) means zero load reached the downstream service — as shown above, the trip call and every half-open probe are real load, and a downstream service "protected" by a breaker still receives periodic real requests the whole time it's unhealthy.
  • Setting reset_timeout far longer than a dependency's typical real recovery time, leaving the breaker open (and rejecting legitimate traffic) long after the dependency actually healed — the fix is probing, not just waiting blindly, which is exactly what half-open does, but only as often as reset_timeout allows.
  • Wrapping a call with a circuit breaker but no fallback behavior for the open state, just propagating the CircuitBreakerError straight to the end user — a breaker's value is partly in enabling a graceful degraded response (cached data, a "try again shortly" message) instead of a generic error, which the calling code still has to implement.
