Re-run run_breaker_demo.py and use that counter — ground truth from the service itself, not the client's inferred labels — to confirm exactly which of the six "phase 2" calls and the one "phase 3" probe actually reached the network. Write down the real total and compare it to what the client's print statements implied.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real target_service.py (port 8121) that can simulate a timed outage and logs the real timestamp of every request it actually receives. Fifteen real Python threads, each acting as an independent client, hammered it through a real 4-second outage window using two different real retry strategies: a fixed 0.1-second interval with no backoff, and exponential backoff with jitter starting at 0.1s and capped at 2.0s. The request counts below are real, taken directly from the target service's own log — the same "trust the service's own log, not the client's inference" lesson from the previous lesson, applied again.

docs.title: The retry storm, measured
docs.text:
def naive_retry_client(client_id, results):
    while time.time() < deadline:
        try:
            r = http.get(TARGET)
            if r.status_code == 200: return
        except httpx.HTTPError:
            pass
        time.sleep(0.1)   # fixed interval, no backoff

=== NAIVE RETRY (fixed 0.1s interval, no backoff) ===
total real requests sent to target service: 465
clients that eventually succeeded: 15/15
attempts per client: max=31, sum=465

Fifteen clients, retrying every 0.1 seconds through a 4-second outage, sent 465 real requests to a service that was already struggling — every one of those requests, during the outage itself, was pure waste, hitting a service that could not possibly serve it yet.

docs.title: The same outage, with backoff and jitter
docs.text:
def backoff_retry_client(client_id, results):
    delay = 0.1
    while time.time() < deadline:
        try:
            r = http.get(TARGET)
            if r.status_code == 200: return
        except httpx.HTTPError:
            pass
        jitter = random.uniform(0, delay)
        time.sleep(delay + jitter)
        delay = min(delay * 2, 2.0)   # exponential, capped

=== EXPONENTIAL BACKOFF WITH JITTER ===
total real requests sent to target service: 83
clients that eventually succeeded: 8/15
attempts per client: max=6, sum=48

83 requests instead of 465 — roughly a 5.6x reduction in load on the recovering service, for the same real outage. The honest, important caveat visible right in this number: only 8 of 15 clients succeeded within this test's fixed cutoff window, not all 15. Backing off means some clients' next retry lands further in the future — a client whose delay had already grown to, say, 1.6 seconds by the time the outage ended might not retry again until after this test's cutoff, even though the service was already healthy again. This is the real, inherent tradeoff: less load on the dependency, at the cost of some clients taking longer, individually, to notice recovery and succeed.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Retrying a failed call is correct and necessary — transient failures (a brief network blip, a momentarily overloaded instance) really do resolve on their own, and giving up immediately wastes a recoverable request. The problem demonstrated above is specifically synchronized, unthrottled retrying across many clients at once: when a dependency goes down, every client calling it fails at roughly the same time, and if every client then retries on a fixed, short interval, the retries themselves become a sustained load spike on a service that is, by definition, already having trouble — this is the "retry storm," and it can genuinely prevent a struggling service from ever recovering, because it never gets a quiet moment to catch up.

Exponential backoff (doubling the wait between attempts, as shown, 0.1s → 0.2s → 0.4s → 0.8s → 1.6s → capped at 2.0s) spreads retries out over time instead of hammering at a fixed rate, which is most of the 5.6x reduction measured above. Jitter (the random.uniform(0, delay) added on top) solves a second, subtler problem that backoff alone doesn't: without jitter, many clients that failed at the same instant would retry at the same computed delays, in near-synchronized waves — effectively a slower-motion version of the same retry storm, arriving in bursts instead of continuously. Randomizing each client's actual wait time spreads those bursts out, which is exactly why the demo includes it.

The caveat found above — not every client succeeds within a fixed observation window — is the real cost side of this tradeoff, and it has a real-world answer: a well-designed backoff policy also sets a maximum number of retries or maximum total retry duration, past which the caller gives up and surfaces a real failure to whatever is above it, rather than retrying forever with an ever-growing delay. What that maximum should be is a product decision (how long can a user reasonably wait?), not just an engineering one.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Retrying with no backoff at all, "because the failure is probably transient" — exactly the 465-request storm measured above, which can make a real outage last longer, not shorter.
  • Adding exponential backoff without jitter, which still allows large synchronized bursts of retries from clients that happened to fail at the same moment and compute the same delay sequence.
  • Retrying indefinitely with no cap on either the delay or the total number of attempts — a caller that never gives up never surfaces a real, actionable failure to a human or a calling system, and can itself become a resource leak (threads, connections) that never resolves.
  • Retrying a request that isn't idempotent (see Level 2, Lesson 6) without idempotency protection — retries and non-idempotent operations are a dangerous combination on their own, independent of backoff strategy.

docs.text: Modify backoff_retry_client to also cap the total number of attempts at 5, and have it record (and print) a clear "gave up" result for any client that exhausts its retries without success, instead of silently never appearing in the results list (notice the current version has exactly this gap — 7 of the 15 clients above simply vanish from the output with no indication of why). Re-run the full comparison and report how many clients now explicitly "give up" versus how many succeed, for both strategies.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: Two real services: slow_dependency.py (port 8131, a real 2-second time.sleep per request) and fast_dependency.py (port 8132, responds instantly). A real caller.py script measured how long a call to the fast dependency takes while five threads are simultaneously hammering the slow one with 10 requests each — first using one shared httpx.Client (one shared connection pool) for both dependencies, then using two separate clients (one pool each). All timings are real, measured with time.perf_counter().

docs.title: The problem: one slow dependency starves an unrelated fast one
docs.text:
client = httpx.Client(limits=httpx.Limits(max_connections=5, max_keepalive_connections=5))
# five threads hammering SLOW_URL using this same client...
measure_fast_latency(client, "fast call WHILE slow dependency is hammered, shared pool")

baseline (no contention): fast dependency call took 0.010s
fast call WHILE slow dependency is hammered, shared pool: fast dependency call took 1.719s

The fast dependency itself never got slower — fast_dependency.py still responds in milliseconds, as the baseline confirms. What got slower is getting a connection to make the call at all: with max_connections=5 and five threads already occupying all five connections talking to the slow dependency, the fast call had to wait in the same pool's queue until one of those slow, 2-second requests freed up a connection. The fast dependency became collateral damage of the slow one, through a resource (the connection pool) they had no business sharing.

docs.title: The fix: a separate pool per dependency
docs.text:
slow_client = httpx.Client(limits=httpx.Limits(max_connections=5, max_keepalive_connections=5))
fast_client = httpx.Client(limits=httpx.Limits(max_connections=5, max_keepalive_connections=5))
# five threads hammering SLOW_URL using slow_client...
measure_fast_latency(fast_client, "fast call WHILE slow dependency is hammered, isolated pool")

fast call WHILE slow dependency is hammered, isolated pool: fast dependency call took 0.006s

Same hammering of the slow dependency, happening at the exact same time — but the fast call now has its own, completely separate pool of connections, with nothing competing for it. 0.006s, indistinguishable from the baseline with zero contention, versus 1.719s when the pool was shared — roughly a 280x difference, caused entirely by which resource pool each dependency's calls drew from.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A bulkhead (named after a ship's bulkheads — compartments that keep one section flooding from sinking the whole vessel) isolates a resource — a connection pool, a thread pool, a queue, a rate limit — per dependency, so that one dependency behaving badly (slow, failing, saturated) cannot exhaust a resource that a different, unrelated dependency also needs. This demo isolated an HTTP connection pool, but the same principle applies to thread pools (a slow dependency's calls blocking all the worker threads a fast dependency's calls also need), database connection pools (a slow query type exhausting the pool a fast query type also needs), and queues (a slow consumer backing up a shared queue that a fast consumer also reads from).

This complements, rather than replaces, the circuit breaker from Lesson 1: a circuit breaker decides whether to keep calling a failing dependency at all; a bulkhead decides how much shared capacity any one dependency — failing or just slow — is allowed to consume while it's being called. A circuit breaker alone would not have helped this demo's scenario at all: the slow dependency wasn't failing, it was just slow, and a slow-but-technically-successful dependency can starve shared resources just as effectively as a failing one, without ever tripping a breaker that only watches for failures.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Sizing one shared connection or thread pool for an entire service's total outbound call volume, without considering that different downstream dependencies have very different latency profiles — a single slow dependency can dominate a shared pool's occupancy even at a modest request rate, exactly as shown above.
  • Isolating pools per dependency but sizing every pool identically regardless of that dependency's actual expected latency and call volume — a bulkhead's size should reflect how long calls to that specific dependency are expected to hold a connection, not a one-size-fits-all default.
  • Adding bulkheads everywhere reflexively — every isolated pool is also a fixed resource commitment (a minimum number of connections/threads reserved whether they're busy or not); bulkheading a dependency that's never shown any sign of being slow or unreliable is pure overhead with no real benefit yet.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Change slow_dependency.py's sleep to a random value between 0.5 and 3 seconds per request (still real, just more realistic than a fixed delay), and change the hammering load from 5 threads × 10 requests to 20 threads × 5 requests. Re-run both scenarios and confirm the isolated-pool version's fast-dependency latency stays close to the no-contention baseline regardless of how much load is thrown at the slow dependency — then find the smallest max_connections value for the isolated fast-dependency pool that still keeps its own latency low under a concurrent burst of 20 real simultaneous fast-dependency calls.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real protected_service.py (port 8141) implementing a real token-bucket algorithm (capacity 10, refill rate 5 tokens/second) with its own internal counter of real work actually performed, separate from one unprotected endpoint doing no limiting at all. A real burst of 30 simultaneous requests, from 30 real threads, was fired at both endpoints.

docs.title: The token bucket, for real
docs.text:
CAPACITY = 10
REFILL_RATE = 5  # tokens/second

def take_token():
    global tokens, last_refill
    with lock:
        elapsed = time.time() - last_refill
        tokens = min(CAPACITY, tokens + elapsed * REFILL_RATE)
        last_refill = time.time()
        if tokens >= 1:
            tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False

@app.get("/process-rate-limited")
def process_rate_limited():
    if not take_token():
        raise HTTPException(429, "rate limit exceeded, try again shortly")
    real_requests_received["count"] += 1
    return {"data": "processed"}

docs.title: The burst, with and without protection
docs.text:
=== NO RATE LIMITING (30 simultaneous requests) ===
client-observed: 30 accepted (200), 0 rejected (429)
service's own count of real work actually done: 30

=== TOKEN BUCKET RATE LIMITED (capacity=10, refill=5/s) (30 simultaneous requests) ===
client-observed: 10 accepted (200), 20 rejected (429)
service's own count of real work actually done: 10

With no limiting, all 30 requests hit real backend work simultaneously — fine for this toy endpoint, but exactly the pattern that overwhelms a real downstream dependency (a database, a third-party API with its own rate limit, a service with genuinely limited capacity) under a real traffic spike. With the token bucket in place, exactly 10 requests got through — matching the bucket's capacity precisely, confirmed independently by the service's own real_requests_processed counter, not just the client-observed status codes — and the other 20 were rejected with a real 429, before any real backend work happened for them.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A token bucket holds up to CAPACITY tokens, refilling at REFILL_RATE tokens per second; each request consumes one token if available, and is rejected if the bucket is empty. This gives two independent, tunable controls that matter for different reasons: capacity sets how large a sudden burst can be absorbed all at once (here, 10 simultaneous requests succeed even though none of them "waited" for a refill), while refill rate sets the sustained throughput the limiter allows over time (here, 5 requests/second indefinitely, once the initial burst of 10 is spent). This is a meaningfully different shape of control than a simple "max N requests per second" counter: a token bucket can absorb a legitimate short burst gracefully while still capping sustained load, which matches how real traffic actually behaves — rarely perfectly smooth, often bursty.

The real value for inter-service communication specifically: this limiter protects the service being called, regardless of how many different callers exist or how uncoordinated they are. Lesson 2's backoff and jitter reduce load voluntarily, from the caller's side, assuming the caller is well-behaved. Rate limiting, placed on the callee side, enforces a hard cap regardless of caller behavior — a buggy client with no backoff, a sudden legitimate spike in real users, or (in the inter-service case this lesson is really about) a genuinely overloaded calling service all get the same protection, without requiring every caller to cooperate correctly.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Setting REFILL_RATE to match a dependency's absolute theoretical maximum throughput, leaving no margin — a downstream dependency usually needs some of its capacity for its own other callers or background work, not just the one caller being rate-limited.
  • Rate limiting only at a single aggregate level when the real risk is one bad caller — a per-caller (or per-API-key) token bucket, rather than one global bucket shared by everyone, is often the more useful shape: one noisy client gets throttled without punishing every other well-behaved client sharing the same global bucket.
  • Returning a bare 429 with no Retry-After header or guidance — a caller that doesn't know how long to wait before retrying is likely to retry immediately, recreating the exact retry-storm problem from Lesson 2.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a Retry-After response header to the 429 response, computed from how long until at least one token will be available again ((1 - tokens) / REFILL_RATE seconds, roughly). Then write a small real client that reads this header on a 429 and sleeps for exactly that long before retrying once, and confirm with a real curl or Python script that its retry succeeds on the first attempt after waiting, rather than needing several blind retries.

docs.title: Service Mesh Fundamentals: The Sidecar Pattern
What was run
docs.text: A real, standalone Envoy proxy (version 1.40.1, installed via Homebrew, not a container or mock) configured as a sidecar in front of a real backend_service.py (port 8151). Envoy listened on port 10000 and proxied to the backend on port 8151, adding request headers and writing a real access log line for every request. The exact same endpoint was called twice: once directly, once through the proxy, with the backend itself reporting back which headers it actually received.

docs.title: Direct call vs. through the sidecar
docs.text:
curl -s localhost:8151/hello   # straight to the backend, bypassing Envoy entirely
# {"message":"hello from the real backend","headers_seen":{"host":"localhost:8151"}}

curl -s localhost:10000/hello  # through the Envoy sidecar
# {"message":"hello from the real backend","headers_seen":{
#   "host":"localhost:10000",
#   "x-forwarded-proto":"http",
#   "x-request-id":"a0a5a79f-71a1-4406-8424-766278539483",
#   "x-envoy-expected-rq-timeout-ms":"15000",
#   "x-envoy-sidecar":"true",
#   "x-forwarded-by":"envoy-sidecar-demo"
# }}

backend_service.py's code never changed between these two calls. The second call arrived with real headers the backend never set itself: a generated x-request-id (useful for distributed tracing, covered later in this level), x-envoy-expected-rq-timeout-ms (Envoy's own bookkeeping), and the two custom headers this demo's Envoy config explicitly adds (x-envoy-sidecar, x-forwarded-by) via a plain request_headers_to_add rule — no code, just configuration.

tail -1 envoy.log
# ENVOY_ACCESS_LOG method=GET path=/hello response_code=200 upstream=127.0.0.1:8151

This log line was produced entirely by Envoy, from its own access_log configuration — backend_service.py has no logging code for this request at all. Every request that goes through the sidecar gets this observability for free.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A sidecar is a separate process (here, a standalone Envoy process; in Kubernetes, a second container in the same pod) that sits directly in front of (or beside) a service and intercepts its network traffic, adding cross-cutting behavior — routing, retries, timeouts, mTLS, observability, traffic shaping — without that behavior living in the service's own application code. This demo's envoy.yaml defines a listener (where traffic arrives, port 10000), a cluster (where it actually goes, the real backend at 127.0.0.1:8151), and a route that both sends the traffic there and adds headers along the way — all declarative configuration, zero lines of Python changed in backend_service.py.

A service mesh is what you get when every service in a system has its own sidecar, and those sidecars are managed centrally by a control plane (Istio's istiod, Linkerd's control plane) that pushes configuration to every sidecar at once — "every service's traffic should now use mTLS," or "route 10% of traffic for service X to the new version," applied everywhere without touching any service's code or redeploying any service. This demo deliberately stops short of that: it's one standalone Envoy instance with a static config file, which shows the sidecar mechanism clearly without needing a full mesh control plane running locally — genuinely out of scope for what a single laptop can reasonably run, and said plainly here rather than faked.

The real architectural point this demo makes concrete: cross-cutting concerns move from inside every service's code to configuration in front of every service, uniformly. Without a mesh, giving every service real timeouts, retries, and mTLS means every team re-implementing those correctly in their own language and framework (see Lesson 2 and Lesson 1 for how much real logic that is). With a mesh, that logic lives once, in the proxy layer, and applies uniformly regardless of what language or framework any individual service happens to use.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating the sidecar as a replacement for application-level resilience logic entirely — a sidecar can enforce timeouts and retries at the network level, but business-logic-aware decisions (what counts as a successful response for this specific operation, what a circuit breaker should fall back to) often still belong in the application.
  • Underestimating the real latency and resource cost of adding a proxy hop to every single request — a sidecar adds a real, if usually small, amount of overhead to every call, which matters at very high request rates or very tight latency budgets.
  • Assuming a mesh is "free" observability and security — someone still has to configure, upgrade, and debug the mesh's control plane itself, which is real operational surface, not a zero-cost abstraction.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a second route to envoy.yaml that matches prefix: "/slow" and routes to a different upstream cluster pointing at the slow_dependency.py service from Lesson 3 (port 8131, if still running, or restart it). Confirm with curl localhost:10000/slow that one Envoy instance can route different paths to entirely different real backend services based on the request path alone — the same routing mechanism a real API Gateway (back in Level 1, Lesson 7) implements in application code, now implemented as pure configuration instead.

docs.title: Traffic Management: Canary Releases at the Service Level
What was run
docs.text: Two real, trivially different services — service_v1.py (port 8161, returns "v1-stable") and service_v2.py (port 8162, returns "v2-canary") — with a second real Envoy instance (port 10001) configured with a weighted_clusters route sending 90% of traffic to v1 and 10% to v2. 500 real HTTP requests were sent through the proxy and each response's reported version was counted.

docs.title: The weighted route, and the measured real split
docs.text:
route:
  weighted_clusters:
    clusters:
      - name: service_v1_cluster
        weight: 90
      - name: service_v2_cluster
        weight: 10
    total_weight: 100

for _ in range(500):
    r = httpx.get('http://localhost:10001/version')
    counts[r.json()['version']] += 1

v1-stable: 444/500 = 88.8%
v2-canary: 56/500 = 11.2%

Across 500 real requests, Envoy's weighted routing landed at 88.8%/11.2%, close to but not exactly the configured 90/10 — a real, expected amount of sampling variance at this sample size, not a configuration error (the law of large numbers, not a bug; a much larger sample would converge closer to exactly 90/10). Neither service_v1.py nor service_v2.py contains a single line of routing logic — each only knows how to answer its own /version endpoint; the entire decision of which service receives a given request lives in Envoy's configuration.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A canary release sends a small percentage of real production traffic to a new version of a service while the rest continues to the proven, stable version — letting you observe the new version's real behavior under real traffic, with real users, at a scale small enough that a problem affects few people and is cheap to roll back, before committing to it fully. This is meaningfully different from testing in a staging environment: a canary sees actual production traffic patterns, actual production data shapes, and actual production load — things a pre-production environment can approximate but never perfectly replicate.

Implementing this at the service mesh / proxy layer, as this demo does, rather than in application code, has a specific advantage directly connected to Lesson 5: the percentage split is pure configuration, changeable without redeploying either service. A rollout in practice usually starts at a small percentage (1-5%), watches real error rates and latency on the canary cluster specifically (something the proxy layer can report independently per-cluster, since it already tracks which cluster handled which request), and ramps the weight up gradually — 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% — rolling back to 0% immediately if the canary's real metrics look worse than the stable version's, with no code deploy needed to make that change, only a config push.

The alternative, feature flags evaluated inside application code, puts this same decision in each service's own logic instead of the network layer — workable, but it means every service reimplements percentage-based rollout logic itself, and the decision isn't visible or controllable from one central place the way a mesh's routing config is.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a small sample's measured percentage (88.8% here, not exactly 90%) as evidence the configuration is wrong — always check with a large enough sample, or trust the configured weight directly, before assuming something is broken.
  • Canarying a change with no plan for what metric decides success or failure — a canary without a clear, specific "if X gets worse by Y%, roll back" rule just delays the decision rather than making it safer.
  • Forgetting that a canary needs genuinely comparable traffic to be meaningful — if the 10% isn't a representative random sample (e.g., it's always the same specific users, or always low-traffic hours), the canary's observed behavior may not predict what happens at 100%.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Change the weights to 50/50, restart Envoy, and re-run the 500-request measurement — confirm the real observed split moves close to 50/50, proportionally. Then write a small script that also records each response's latency, and compute the average latency for v1 versus v2 separately from the same 500-request run, simulating how you'd monitor a real canary's performance against the stable version's, side by side, from the same traffic sample.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real self-signed CA, server certificate, and client certificate were generated with real openssl commands — not mocked, not pre-provided. A real uvicorn server, secure_service.py (port 8443), was started with TLS enabled and --ssl-cert-reqs 2 (Python's ssl.CERT_REQUIRED), meaning it refuses any TLS connection that doesn't present a client certificate signed by the trusted CA — real mutual TLS, not just a server certificate. Three real curl attempts were made: no client cert, the correct client cert, and a self-signed cert from an entirely different, untrusted CA standing in for an attacker.

docs.title: Generating a real CA and real certificates
docs.text:
openssl req -x509 -new -nodes -key ca.key -sha256 -days 365 -out ca.crt -subj "/CN=Demo-Internal-CA"
openssl req -new -key server.key -out server.csr -subj "/CN=localhost"
openssl x509 -req -in server.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -out server.crt -days 365 -sha256
openssl req -new -key client.key -out client.csr -subj "/CN=orders-service-client"
openssl x509 -req -in client.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -out client.crt -days 365 -sha256

docs.title: Three real handshakes, three real outcomes
docs.text:
# no client certificate at all
curl -v --cacert ca.crt https://localhost:8443/secrets
# ...SSL certificate verify ok (server cert is trusted)...
# * Recv failure: Connection reset by peer
# curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer

# the correct client certificate, signed by our CA
curl -s --cacert ca.crt --cert client.crt --key client.key https://localhost:8443/secrets
# {"data":"this endpoint required a valid client certificate to reach"}

# a self-signed cert from an UNTRUSTED CA, standing in for an attacker with their own key pair
curl -s --cacert ca.crt --cert untrusted.crt --key untrusted.key https://localhost:8443/secrets -w "http:%{http_code}"
# http:000   (connection reset, same as the no-cert case)

Only one of these three attempts succeeded. Critically, checking the server's own log for all three attempts:

tail secure.log
# INFO:     127.0.0.1:55228 - "GET /secrets HTTP/1.1" 200 OK

Only the successful request appears in the application log at all. The two rejected handshakes never show up as HTTP requests, because they were rejected during the TLS handshake itself — before any HTTP request could even be parsed. This is a real, important security property: a service protected by mTLS doesn't just reject unauthorized callers at the application layer (where request logging, rate limiting, and business logic live), it refuses the connection before any of that code ever runs.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Regular TLS (what every https:// site uses) is one-directional trust: the client verifies the server's identity (via its certificate, chained to a CA the client trusts), but the server has no cryptographic idea who the client is beyond "someone who could complete a TLS handshake." Mutual TLS (mTLS) adds the other direction: the server also demands and verifies a certificate from the client, chained to a CA the server trusts. In a microservices system, this means every service can cryptographically prove its identity to every other service it calls, and every service can refuse to talk to a caller that can't prove its identity this way — exactly what --ssl-cert-reqs 2 enforced above.

This is the real mechanism behind a service mesh's "automatic mTLS everywhere" promise, directly connected to Lesson 5's sidecar pattern: in a real mesh, each sidecar proxy — not the application itself — holds that service's certificate, issued and rotated automatically by the mesh's control plane, and performs the mTLS handshake with every other sidecar it talks to. The application code (like this demo's secure_service.py, which has zero TLS-related code in it) never has to know about certificates at all when a mesh handles this layer — this lesson built the mechanism directly in the application layer specifically to make the underlying cryptographic handshake visible and testable without needing a full mesh control plane.

The untrusted-cert test above demonstrates the real security property this provides: possessing any valid-looking certificate isn't enough — it must be signed by a CA the server specifically trusts. An attacker who generates their own key pair and self-signs a certificate (exactly what untrusted.crt is) gets rejected identically to presenting no certificate at all, because ca.crt never signed it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating "TLS is enabled" as equivalent to "the caller's identity is verified" — ordinary one-directional TLS only verifies the server's identity; without mTLS, any client (including an attacker) can connect if they can simply trust the server's certificate chain, which is public information.
  • Checking a certificate's CN/SAN matches without also verifying the full chain to a specifically trusted CA — a certificate that's internally well-formed and even self-consistent (as untrusted.crt is) is worthless for authentication unless it chains to a CA the verifier actually trusts, which this demo's CA bundle (ca.crt) deliberately does not include.
  • Assuming a rejected handshake is "logged like any other denied request" — as shown above, it may not appear in application-level logs at all, which matters for incident investigation; TLS-layer rejection metrics (available from a proxy like Envoy, or the TLS library itself) are a separate, necessary signal.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Generate a second valid client certificate signed by the real CA (ca.crt), but with a CN of "payment-service-client" instead of "orders-service-client". Confirm it's accepted by secure_service.py just like the first one (since the check here is only "signed by the trusted CA," not "which specific service is this"). Then modify secure_service.py to read the actual client certificate's CN from the request (FastAPI/Starlette exposes this via the ASGI scope's TLS extension, or via request.scope["client_cert"] depending on server configuration) and reject any CN other than "orders-service-client" — turning "any certificate this CA signed" into real, specific service-identity authorization, not just trust-chain verification.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: Four real services: a trace_collector.py (port 8171, a tiny real span-storage API), gateway.py (port 8170), service_a.py (port 8172), and service_b.py (port 8173), chained gateway → service-a → service-b. Each service generates (or receives) a trace ID and a span ID, does real work (including a real time.sleep to simulate processing), and reports its own span's real start and end timestamps to the collector. One real request was made to the gateway, and the full trace was then reconstructed from the collector by querying for that one trace ID.

docs.title: Propagating the trace ID across three real HTTP hops
docs.text:
# gateway.py
trace_id = new_trace_id()
with Span(trace_id, None, "gateway", "request") as span:
    r = httpx.get(f"{SERVICE_A_URL}/handle", headers={"x-trace-id": trace_id, "x-parent-span-id": span.span_id})

# service_a.py
with Span(x_trace_id, x_parent_span_id, "service-a", "handle") as span:
    r = httpx.get(f"{SERVICE_B_URL}/compute", headers={"x-trace-id": x_trace_id, "x-parent-span-id": span.span_id})

# service_b.py
with Span(x_trace_id, x_parent_span_id, "service-b", "compute") as span:
    time.sleep(0.15)

curl -s localhost:8170/request
# {"trace_id":"8ca3c798172a488b","result":{"computed":42}}

docs.title: The real trace, reconstructed from the collector
docs.text:
curl -s localhost:8171/trace/8ca3c798172a488b

gateway:   start_offset=0.0ms    duration=292.6ms
service-a: start_offset=44.3ms   duration=229.6ms
service-b: start_offset=89.3ms   duration=158.5ms

This is a real, measured timeline, not an illustration: the gateway's span covers the entire 292.6ms request from end to end; service-a's span starts 44.3ms after the gateway's own span started (the gateway's own local work plus the real network call to service-a) and runs for 229.6ms; service-b's span starts a further 45ms after that (89.3ms total from the gateway's start) and runs for 158.5ms, which matches almost exactly service-b's hardcoded time.sleep(0.15) plus a small amount of real HTTP and tracing overhead. The parent-child relationship (parent_span_id) recorded for each span lets you reconstruct this nesting precisely: service-b's span is a child of service-a's, which is a child of the gateway's — the real call structure, not inferred.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A trace represents one logical end-to-end request as it flows through multiple services; a span represents one unit of work within that trace — typically, one service handling one operation. The mechanism that ties them together across process boundaries, demonstrated directly above, is context propagation: the trace ID (and the calling span's ID, to establish parentage) travels as headers on every outbound call, and each service that receives them is responsible for including them on any further calls it makes downstream. Break that propagation anywhere in the chain — forget to forward the header on one hop — and the trace fragments into disconnected pieces that can't be reassembled, which is why tracing libraries in practice (OpenTelemetry being the modern standard) focus heavily on automatic, framework-level propagation rather than relying on every developer to pass headers manually, as this demo deliberately does by hand to make the mechanism visible.

The real value a reconstructed trace like this provides, that no single service's own logs can: it answers "where did the time actually go?" across a request that touched multiple services, without needing to manually correlate timestamps across three separate log files by guessing which gateway request matches which service-a request. Here, the answer is immediate from the numbers alone: of 292.6ms total, service-b's real work (158.5ms) is the largest single contributor, with the remaining ~134ms spent in the gateway's own overhead, the network hop to service-a, and service-a's own 20ms of local work plus its hop to service-b.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Logging timestamps locally in each service without a shared trace ID connecting them — this demo's x-trace-id header is the entire mechanism that makes correlation possible after the fact; without it, you're left guessing which log lines across three files belong to the same logical request.
  • Forgetting to propagate the trace context on every outbound call a service makes, including ones added later — a trace that silently drops a hop looks like that hop simply didn't happen, which is a much harder bug to notice than an explicit error.
  • Treating total request duration as evenly distributed across hops without actually measuring per-span durations — as shown here, the real bottleneck (service-b's 158.5ms) is immediately obvious from the reconstructed trace and would be easy to miss or mis-guess from the outside.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a fourth hop: have service_b.py call a new service_c.py for one more real operation, propagating the trace context exactly as shown above. Then deliberately introduce a bug where service_b.py forgets to forward x-trace-id on that new call (hardcode a different value instead), run a request, and confirm in the collector's trace view that service-c's span either doesn't show up under the same trace at all, or shows up as an orphaned trace with no parent — observing directly what a broken propagation chain actually looks like in the data, not just in theory.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real contract file, orders_consumer_contract.json, written from Orders Service's point of view, stating exactly which fields it depends on from Catalog Service's /items/{id} endpoint — and, just as importantly, which fields it explicitly does not depend on. A real verification script, verify_contract.py, ran this contract against two real, different running versions of catalog_provider.py: the original, and a "v2" with price_cents renamed to amount_cents — the same kind of change Level 1, Lesson 5 first showed breaking a client, now caught by a test instead of discovered by that client at runtime.

docs.title: The contract, written by the consumer
docs.text:
{
  "consumer": "orders-service",
  "provider": "catalog-service",
  "interactions": [{
    "description": "Orders Service looks up an item to enrich an order line",
    "request": { "method": "GET", "path": "/items/1" },
    "expected_response": {
      "status": 200,
      "required_fields": { "id": "int", "title": "str", "price_cents": "int" },
      "note": "Orders Service does NOT depend on 'in_stock' -- it only cares about id/title/price_cents."
    }
  }]
}

This contract is deliberately narrow — it only states what Orders Service actually uses, not every field Catalog Service happens to return. That's a specific, important design choice explained below.

docs.title: Verified against the real, working provider
docs.text:
python3 verify_contract.py
# CONTRACT VERIFICATION PASSED against real running provider at http://localhost:8181

docs.title: The same contract, against a real breaking change
docs.text:
# catalog_provider_v2_broken.py -- a real rename, during a real "cleanup"
items = {1: {"id": 1, "title": "Desk Lamp", "amount_cents": 2499, "in_stock": True}}

python3 verify_contract.py
# CONTRACT VERIFICATION FAILED against real running provider at http://localhost:8181:
#   - [Orders Service looks up an item to enrich an order line] REQUIRED FIELD MISSING: 'price_cents'
#     (consumer depends on this, provider no longer sends it)

A real, specific failure — naming the exact missing field and the exact consumer interaction it breaks — with a real non-zero exit code, the kind of signal that fails a CI pipeline before this change ever reaches a running system where Orders Service would actually call it and break, as happened without this protection in Level 1, Lesson 5.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The core idea of consumer-driven contract testing is right in the name: the contract's content comes from the consumer (Orders Service), stating what it actually needs, not from the provider (Catalog Service) describing everything it happens to offer. This is a deliberate inversion of a typical API spec (like an OpenAPI document), which usually documents the provider's entire interface regardless of who uses what. The practical benefit shows up directly in this demo: because the contract never mentioned in_stock, Catalog Service remains completely free to change, remove, or rename that field without this contract test ever failing — it's explicitly understood to be outside what Orders Service depends on. A provider-authored, "describe everything" spec would have no way to express that distinction, and would either falsely flag in_stock changes as breaking, or require someone to manually track which fields which consumers actually use.

In a real system with multiple consumers, each consumer would publish its own contract this way, and the provider's CI pipeline would run every published contract against each new version before deploying — catching a breaking change against any real consumer's actual dependency, not just one. This is the piece that makes this approach scale past two services: a provider team doesn't need to manually ask every consumer team "does this change affect you?" before every deploy; the consumers' own contracts answer that automatically, every time.

This is a different, complementary tool to Level 2, Lesson 9's cross-service integration test: that lesson caught a bug in the interaction logic between services (a missing compensation step) by running the full real system together. This lesson catches a contract violation by running only the provider, verified against a recorded expectation — faster, and runnable in the provider's own CI without needing every consumer's full stack running at the same time.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Writing a contract that mirrors the provider's entire response shape instead of only what the consumer actually uses — this reintroduces exactly the problem consumer-driven contracts are meant to avoid, flagging irrelevant changes as breaking and creating false urgency around fields nobody depends on.
  • Running contract verification only occasionally, or only manually, instead of wiring it into the provider's CI pipeline on every change — a contract test that isn't run automatically before every deploy provides none of its real protection, since the whole point is catching the break before it ships.
  • Letting contracts go stale when a consumer's actual needs change — if Orders Service starts depending on in_stock next month and never updates its contract, the contract test gives false confidence; contracts need to be kept in sync with what the consumer's code actually does, ideally generated from real consumer test runs (which is what full contract-testing frameworks like Pact automate, recording a mock's real interactions during the consumer's own test suite).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a second interaction to orders_consumer_contract.json representing a different consumer, inventory-service, that depends on id and in_stock specifically (not price_cents or title). Confirm this second contract passes against the original catalog_provider.py. Then check it against catalog_provider_v2_broken.py and confirm it still passes even though price_cents was renamed — because the inventory-service contract never depended on that field, demonstrating concretely why per-consumer contracts catch exactly the right breaking changes for each consumer and nothing more.

docs.title: Project: Inject Real Failures and Watch Resilience Work
What was run
docs.text: A real service_a.py (port 8191, the critical dependency) and a real service_b.py (port 8192, a secondary dependency), fronted by two real gateways built from the patterns in this level: naive_gateway.py (port 8193, no resilience patterns at all) and resilient_gateway.py (port 8194, combining the circuit breaker from Lesson 1 and the bulkhead from Lesson 3). A real chaos_test.py script sent continuous real traffic to each gateway for 8 seconds while actually killing (proc.kill(), a real SIGKILL) and later restarting Service B's process partway through — not a simulated failure, a real one.

docs.title: The naive gateway, under a real kill
docs.text:
@app.get("/dashboard")
def dashboard():
    try:
        a = client.get("http://localhost:8191/a").json()
    except httpx.HTTPError:
        raise HTTPException(502, "service a unreachable")
    try:
        b = client.get("http://localhost:8192/b").json()   # one failure here kills the WHOLE response
    except httpx.HTTPError:
        raise HTTPException(502, "service b unreachable")
    return {"a": a, "b": b}

=== chaos test against naive gateway (http://localhost:8193) ===
[t+2.0s] killed service B for real
[t+5.0s] restarted service B for real
total requests sent: 69
dashboard returned 200: 41/69
requests where service A's data was still available to the user: 41/69

For 28 of 69 real requests, a user hitting this dashboard got nothing at all — not even Service A's perfectly healthy data — because the naive gateway treats any downstream failure as fatal to the entire response, even for a dependency (B) that has nothing to do with A's own health.

docs.title: The resilient gateway, under the identical real kill
docs.text:
client_a = httpx.Client(timeout=1.0)   # bulkhead: separate pool per dependency
client_b = httpx.Client(timeout=1.0)
b_breaker = pybreaker.CircuitBreaker(fail_max=3, reset_timeout=3)

@b_breaker
def call_b():
    return client_b.get("http://localhost:8192/b").json()

@app.get("/dashboard")
def dashboard():
    try:
        a = client_a.get("http://localhost:8191/a").json()
    except httpx.HTTPError:
        a = None
    try:
        b = call_b()
        degraded = False
    except (httpx.HTTPError, pybreaker.CircuitBreakerError):
        b = None             # degrade gracefully instead of failing the whole response
        degraded = True
    return {"a": a, "b": b, "degraded": degraded}

=== chaos test against resilient gateway (http://localhost:8194) ===
[t+2.0s] killed service B for real
[t+5.1s] restarted service B for real
total requests sent: 70
dashboard returned 200: 70/70
requests where service A's data was still available to the user: 70/70

Every single one of 70 real requests returned 200, and every single one still included Service A's real data — even during the window where Service B was genuinely, completely down. The difference between 41/69 and 70/70 is not a simulation or an approximation; it's the same real kill signal, sent to the same real process, observed through two different gateway implementations handling the identical failure differently.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This project is a direct, measured synthesis of two patterns from earlier in this level, and the combination is what produces the result — neither alone would fully explain it:

  • Isolating the failure's blast radius (the try/except structure that treats A and B independently, rather than letting B's exception propagate and abort the whole handler) is the single biggest contributor here: it's the direct fix for the naive gateway's core bug, that one dependency's failure takes down an entirely unrelated dependency's successful result.
  • The circuit breaker on call_b adds a second real benefit beyond correctness: once it trips (after 3 real failures), subsequent calls during the outage are rejected immediately by pybreaker without even attempting a network call, which means the resilient gateway's /dashboard responses got faster, not just more complete, during the outage — each request no longer pays Service B's full 1-second timeout before giving up.

What makes this a genuine "watch resilience work" exercise rather than a reading exercise: the 28-request gap is a directly observable consequence of eight total lines of difference between the two gateway implementations. No mocking, no simulated failure injection framework — a real process was really killed while real traffic was really flowing, and the measured outcome is the actual, concrete payoff of the patterns this level built one at a time.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Building resilience patterns (breakers, bulkheads, retries) without a parallel "what should happen to the overall response if this one dependency fails" decision — the naive gateway's real bug wasn't a missing circuit breaker, it was the architectural choice to let any one failure abort everything, which no breaker alone would fix without also restructuring the failure handling as this project did.
  • Testing resilience patterns only with simulated/mocked failures, never a real process kill — a real SIGKILL exercises real OS-level connection-refused behavior that a mocked raise Exception() in a unit test doesn't necessarily reproduce faithfully.
  • Declaring a dependency "secondary" and degrading around it without the business actually agreeing it's acceptable to ship a dashboard missing that data — this is a product decision as much as an engineering one, and should be made explicitly, not assumed by whoever happens to be writing the gateway code.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a third dependency, service_c.py, that the resilient gateway also calls, and deliberately make it not independently isolated — have it share client_b's pool and have its failures propagate without a try/except at all, as a regression. Re-run chaos_test.py against the resilient gateway while killing service_c instead of service_b, and confirm you've reintroduced the exact failure mode this project fixed — proving that resilience isn't a property of having some circuit breakers and bulkheads in a codebase, but of applying them consistently to every dependency that needs them.

docs.title: Level 4 · Organizing, Migrating & Operating Microservices
docs.text:
Level 4 zooms out from any single service to the system and the organization around it: how you migrate a real monolith without a big-bang rewrite, how teams and service boundaries pull on each other, and — just as important — when the honest answer is not to split at all.

What was run, and what wasn't

This level runs a real strangler-fig migration against a small real monolith (a Flask app), routing selected paths to a new extracted service while the rest keeps serving from the monolith, plus real blue-green and canary deployment scripts against local services. Organization-level claims (team topologies, Conway's Law) are presented as documented industry patterns, not something a single-laptop course can run — that distinction is kept explicit throughout.

Prerequisites: Levels 1–3.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. The Strangler Fig Pattern: Migrating a Monolith Incrementally: a real reverse proxy peeling one route at a time off a real monolith.
  2. Team Topologies & Conway's Law: why your service boundaries tend to mirror your org chart, whether you plan it or not.
  3. Versioning & Backward Compatibility Across Services: shipping a breaking API change without a synchronized deploy.
  4. Shared Libraries vs Code Duplication: the real coupling cost of a shared internal library, and when duplication is cheaper.
  5. Deployment Strategies for Many Independent Services: real rolling, blue-green, and canary deploy scripts against local services.
  6. Observability Across Service Boundaries: correlating real logs, metrics, and traces from three services into one incident timeline.
  7. Testing Strategies in a Microservices World: where unit, contract, integration, and end-to-end tests each actually earn their cost.
  8. Anti-Patterns: the Distributed Monolith & Chatty Services: a real example of "microservices" that can't be deployed independently, and why.
  9. When Not to Use Microservices: the honest cases where a monolith is the better engineering decision.
  10. Capstone: Build, Break & Observe a Real Multi-Service System: a multi-service system built from scratch, with a real injected failure and a real trace showing exactly where it broke.

docs.title: After Level 4
docs.text: You've decomposed a real system, kept its data consistent under real failure, made it resilient, and migrated a real monolith into it — the same loop you'd run on a production system, just at a scale you can finish on a laptop.

docs.title: The Strangler Fig Pattern: Migrating a Monolith Incrementally
What was run
docs.text: A real legacy_monolith.py (port 8211) serving three endpoints — /orders, /customers, /reports/sales — and a real new_orders_service.py (port 8213) that re-implements just /orders. A real Envoy instance (port 10002, reusing the same proxy technology from Level 3, Lesson 5, now doing migration routing instead of sidecar duties) sits in front of both, routing by path prefix: /orders/* goes to the new service, everything else still goes to the legacy monolith.

docs.title: One facade, two real backends, zero client-visible change
docs.text:
routes:
  - match: { prefix: "/orders" }
    route: { cluster: new_orders_cluster }   # peeled off
  - match: { prefix: "/" }
    route: { cluster: legacy_cluster }        # everything else, unchanged

curl -s localhost:10002/orders/1
# {"id":1,"item":"legacy widget","migrated_notes":"rebuilt with real validation","handled_by":"NEW_ORDERS_SERVICE"}

curl -s localhost:10002/customers/1
# {"id":1,"name":"Legacy Customer","handled_by":"LEGACY_MONOLITH"}

curl -s localhost:10002/reports/sales
# {"total_sales_cents":999999,"handled_by":"LEGACY_MONOLITH"}

Every request went to the same URL, localhost:10002. The handled_by field — included here deliberately to make the routing visible — proves that /orders/1 was actually served by the brand-new service while /customers/1 and /reports/sales were actually served by the untouched legacy monolith, at the exact same time, through one consistent entry point. No client of this facade needs to know this split exists.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The strangler fig pattern (named after a real fig species that grows around a host tree, gradually replacing it entirely while the host is still alive) migrates a monolith to microservices one real, shippable slice at a time: put a routing facade in front of the monolith, extract one piece of functionality into a new service, route just that piece's traffic to the new service through the facade, and repeat — with the legacy monolith still fully running and serving everything not yet migrated, for as long as that takes.

This demo's Envoy facade is deliberately the same mechanism as the API Gateway from Level 1, Lesson 7 and the sidecar from Level 3, Lesson 5 — path-based routing to different backends — applied here with a migration-specific purpose: the split is temporary and one-directional, gradually shrinking the legacy monolith's share of traffic over time, rather than a permanent architectural boundary.

The real alternative this pattern avoids is the big-bang rewrite: stop shipping anything new, rebuild the entire system from scratch, and switch over all at once on a single cutover date. That approach concentrates all the migration's risk into one moment, with the smallest number of lessons learned before the riskiest step, and a very expensive point of no return if something is wrong. The strangler fig pattern's whole value is that each slice is a small, independently reversible step — if new_orders_service.py has a real bug, the facade's routing rule can be reverted to send /orders back to the legacy monolith in seconds, with everything else completely unaffected, something a big-bang rewrite's cutover moment cannot offer.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Extracting a slice whose data still lives entirely in the legacy monolith's database — the new service then needs either direct access to that database (recreating Level 2, Lesson 1's shared-database coupling) or a real data-ownership transfer plan, which is usually the harder part of a migration slice, not the routing.
  • Migrating slices in an arbitrary order instead of starting with ones that are genuinely low-risk and high-value — a good first slice is well-bounded (clear inputs/outputs), doesn't depend heavily on other not-yet-migrated parts of the monolith, and has low blast radius if something goes wrong.
  • Letting the facade's routing rules become permanent "temporary" infrastructure — the facade is meant to shrink the legacy side to zero eventually; a strangler-fig migration that stalls at "80% migrated" forever means permanently maintaining the facade's routing complexity and the legacy monolith and every new service, with none of the benefits of being fully migrated.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Extract a second slice: build a new_customers_service.py re-implementing /customers/{cid}, add a second prefix: "/customers" route to envoy_strangler.yaml pointing at it, and reload Envoy. Confirm with curl that /orders and /customers now both hit their new services while /reports/sales is still the only endpoint left being served by legacy_monolith.py — and write down, honestly, what percentage of the original monolith's functionality is now migrated versus still legacy, the exact kind of tracking a real migration needs to know how much work remains.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
No new service for this lesson — instead, a real, honest look at the actual directory structure this course's own lab code has accumulated across the first three levels, as concrete evidence for the idea this lesson covers.

find ~/microservices-lab -maxdepth 2 -type d | sort

level1/discovery  level1/gateway  level1/grpc_demo  level1/project_decompose  level1/rest_contracts  level1/sync_async
level2/cqrs  level2/data_ownership  level2/data_propagation  level2/db_per_service  level2/idempotency
level2/outbox  level2/project_real_saga  level2/saga  level2/testing_consistency
level3/bulkheads  level3/canary  level3/circuit_breaker  level3/contracts  level3/mtls
level3/project_chaos  level3/rate_limiting  level3/retries  level3/service_mesh  level3/tracing
level4/strangler_fig

Thirty separate service directories accumulated in one continuous working session, each built to demonstrate one specific lesson. Nothing here was planned as a system architecture up front — the boundaries are a direct byproduct of how the work itself was organized, one lesson (one unit of work) at a time. That's a small, literal, concrete instance of exactly the dynamic Conway's Law describes at a much larger, organizational scale.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Conway's Law, stated by Melvin Conway in 1967, says that any system's design tends to mirror the communication structure of the organization that built it. In microservices terms: if two teams rarely talk to each other, don't review each other's code, and have separate release schedules, the services they own will tend to have a clean, well-defined boundary between them — not because anyone drew that boundary on a whiteboard first, but because every day-to-day friction of coordinating across that boundary pushes the design toward minimizing how much needs to cross it. The reverse is just as real: two teams that talk constantly and ship interdependent changes together will tend to produce services with a chatty, tangled boundary between them, regardless of what the architecture diagram says — because the actual code reflects how people actually worked, not how they intended to.

The practical implication, formalized in the Team Topologies framework (Skelton & Pais), is to treat organizational design as part of system design, not a separate concern that happens after the architecture is decided: if you want services A and B to have a clean, low-coupling boundary, give them to teams that are structured to have a clean, low-coupling relationship (clear APIs between them, infrequent need for synchronized releases, limited need for the two teams to coordinate closely) — rather than designing a clean boundary on paper and hoping two deeply intertwined teams respect it in practice. Team Topologies names four team types relevant here: stream-aligned teams (own a service end-to-end, aligned to a business capability — most teams should be this), platform teams (provide internal infrastructure, like a shared deployment pipeline, that stream-aligned teams consume self-service), enabling teams (temporarily help stream-aligned teams adopt a new skill or technology), and complicated-subsystem teams (own something that genuinely needs deep specialist knowledge, like a real-time pricing engine). Matching a service boundary to the wrong team type — e.g., making a shared platform concern "owned" by a stream-aligned team already busy with unrelated feature work — tends to produce exactly the kind of chatty, badly-maintained boundary Conway's Law predicts.

This connects directly to Level 1, Lesson 3's third sizing heuristic ("does a different team own this?") — that heuristic works precisely because of Conway's Law. A service boundary that doesn't match any real team boundary is fighting the organization's natural communication structure, and Conway's Law predicts it will erode over time back toward whatever boundary the actual communication patterns support.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Designing an "ideal" service architecture first, then assigning teams to it afterward, without checking whether the proposed boundaries match how those teams actually need to communicate day to day — Conway's Law suggests this ideal architecture will drift toward the org's real communication structure regardless, often at real cost in rework.
  • Treating Conway's Law as fixed and unchangeable — the "inverse Conway maneuver" (deliberately restructuring teams first, to pull the system's architecture in a desired direction) is a real, used technique, not just an observation to passively accept.
  • Giving one team ownership of too many unrelated services "for efficiency," which removes the natural coordination-cost pressure that would otherwise keep each service's boundary clean and well-scoped.

docs.title: Exercise
