Write down one concrete way their boundary might have turned out differently — tighter or looser — if they had instead been built by two different, loosely-coordinating people, each only seeing the other's work through a published API, with no shared context about how the other one was implemented.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real catalog_versioned.py (port 8221) extending the /v1 vs /v2 split from Level 1, Lesson 5 with real deprecation signaling: standard Deprecation and Sunset HTTP response headers (from RFC 8594) on the old version, plus a real server-side log of every actual call /v1 receives — the concrete mechanism a real team would use to answer "is it actually safe to delete this yet?"

docs.title: Announcing deprecation with real, standard headers
docs.text:
@app.get("/v1/items/{item_id}")
def get_item_v1(item_id: int, response: Response):
    v1_usage_log.append(time.time())
    response.headers["Deprecation"] = "true"
    response.headers["Sunset"] = "Wed, 01 Jan 2027 00:00:00 GMT"
    response.headers["Link"] = '</v2/items/{}>; rel="successor-version"'.format(item_id)

curl -sD - localhost:8221/v1/items/1
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK
# deprecation: true
# sunset: Wed, 01 Jan 2027 00:00:00 GMT
# link: </v2/items/1>; rel="successor-version"
#
# {"id":1,"title":"Desk Lamp","price":24.99}

The old endpoint still works exactly as before — this is backward compatibility, not a breaking removal — but every caller that actually inspects response headers (or runs tooling that does) now gets a real, standardized signal: this version is going away, here's roughly when, and here's where to migrate to.

docs.title: Proving whether it's actually safe to remove
docs.text:
@app.get("/v1-usage-report")
def v1_usage_report():
    last_24h = [t for t in v1_usage_log if time.time() - t < 86400]
    return {"total_v1_calls_ever_recorded": len(v1_usage_log), "v1_calls_last_24h": len(last_24h),
            "safe_to_remove_v1": len(last_24h) == 0}

# a "legacy client we forgot about" makes a few real calls to v1...
curl -s localhost:8221/v1-usage-report
# {"total_v1_calls_ever_recorded":4,"v1_calls_last_24h":4,"safe_to_remove_v1":false}

This is the real, concrete answer to a question that's otherwise just a guess: /v1 has had 4 real calls in the last 24 hours, so safe_to_remove_v1 is honestly false. Without this kind of real usage tracking, a team deciding whether to delete /v1 is working from assumption ("probably nobody uses this anymore") rather than evidence — and the cost of being wrong is a real outage for whichever caller was still depending on it.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Backward compatibility and versioning together answer two separate, related questions: how do you let an API evolve without breaking existing callers (Level 1, Lesson 5's /v1 vs /v2 split), and how do you eventually retire an old version safely, once it exists, which is what this lesson adds. The second question is harder than it looks, because the one piece of information you actually need — "does anyone still call this?" — isn't visible from the API's code at all; it's only visible from real, ongoing traffic data, exactly what v1_usage_log captures here.

The Deprecation and Sunset headers are a real, standardized (RFC 8594) way to communicate retirement plans to automated clients, not just to humans reading a changelog — a well-behaved client library can check for Deprecation: true and log a warning, or alert on a dashboard, entirely automatically, without a human needing to notice a blog post. This is the HTTP-level analog of a compiler deprecation warning: the information is attached to the thing itself, at the point of use, rather than living only in separate documentation that's easy to miss.

Putting these two pieces together gives a complete, real lifecycle: announce deprecation with real timestamps and a pointer to the replacement (this lesson's headers), keep the old version fully functional during the deprecation window (standard backward compatibility), and use real traffic data — not a guess, not an announcement date alone — to decide when actual removal is safe. The announced sunset date (January 2027 above) is a target, not a guarantee; the actual decision to remove /v1 should wait for the usage data to confirm it, exactly as safe_to_remove_v1 does here.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Announcing a sunset date and then removing the old version on that date regardless of what real usage data shows — an announced deadline is a target to work toward, not a substitute for checking whether removal is actually safe.
  • Adding deprecation headers but never actually logging or monitoring real usage of the deprecated endpoint — without the usage log this lesson built, the headers alone tell you nothing about whether anyone's actually reading them or still depending on the old version.
  • Deprecating a version with no working, documented replacement already available — the Link: successor-version header above only has value if /v2 is a real, complete, production-ready substitute by the time /v1 starts warning callers away from itself.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Extend v1_usage_log to record which caller (via a real User-Agent or a custom client-identifying header) made each call, not just when. Simulate three different "client" identities calling /v1 with different header values, then extend /v1-usage-report to list each distinct caller still active in the last 24 hours — turning "is it safe to remove" into "here is exactly who still needs to migrate before it's safe," the real, actionable version of this question a team actually needs answered before deleting anything.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real, pip-installable local package, shop-common (built with a real pyproject.toml and installed with pip install -e .), providing one function, format_price(), imported by two real, otherwise-unrelated services: orders_service.py (port 8231) and newsletter_service.py (port 8232). The shared package was then upgraded in place from a real v1.0.0 to a real v2.0.0 with a breaking change, and both services were restarted — the real equivalent of a shared library's new version being rolled out everywhere it's used.

docs.title: Both services, sharing one real installed package
docs.text:
# shop_common/__init__.py, v1.0.0
def format_price(cents: int) -> str:
    return f"${cents/100:.2f}"

# orders_service.py
from shop_common import format_price
return {"item": "keyboard", "price_display": format_price(5000)}

# newsletter_service.py
from shop_common import format_price
return {"item": "desk lamp", "price_display": format_price(2499)}

curl -s localhost:8231/orders/1/receipt
# {"item":"keyboard","price_display":"$50.00"}
curl -s localhost:8232/newsletter/deal-of-the-day
# {"item":"desk lamp","price_display":"$24.99"}

Both services' responses used the exact same shared formatting logic — real, working code reuse, no duplicated f"${cents/100:.2f}" string floating around in two places.

docs.title: One upgrade, two services broken at the same instant
docs.text:
# shop_common/__init__.py, v2.0.0 -- the orders team didn't ask for this, didn't review it
def format_price(cents: int) -> dict:
    return {"currency": "USD", "amount": round(cents / 100, 2)}

# after restarting BOTH services to pick up the new shared package version:
curl -s localhost:8231/orders/1/receipt
# {"item":"keyboard","price_display":{"currency":"USD","amount":50.0}}

curl -s localhost:8232/newsletter/deal-of-the-day
# {"item":"desk lamp","price_display":{"currency":"USD","amount":24.99}}

Neither service's own code changed by a single character. Both services' real, public JSON contracts changed shape — price_display went from a plain string to a nested object — at exactly the same moment, because both depend on the same installed copy of the same function. Any real client of either service that expected price_display to be a string (to display it directly, say) breaks identically in both places, simultaneously, from a change neither service's own team necessarily reviewed as "a change to my service's API."

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Sharing code between services through a real library (as opposed to each service keeping its own, possibly duplicated, copy of the same logic) gives real, genuine benefits: write the logic once, fix a bug in one place instead of N places, and get consistent behavior everywhere it's used — exactly what the v1.0.0 scenario demonstrated working correctly. The real cost, demonstrated by the v2.0.0 upgrade, is that a shared library creates a deployment-coupling dependency between every service that uses it, even services that have nothing else to do with each other, as orders_service.py and newsletter_service.py don't. Upgrading the library is not a decision any one service's team can make in isolation — it silently affects every consumer, whether or not that consumer's team reviewed, tested against, or even knew about the change.

This is directly analogous to the shared-database problem from Level 2, Lesson 1: there, two services sharing one database table were coupled through an invisible schema dependency; here, two services sharing one library are coupled through an invisible function-signature dependency. The fix follows the same shape too — duplication, deliberately chosen, removes the coupling entirely: if orders_service.py and newsletter_service.py had each kept their own private copy of a price-formatting function, upgrading one would never affect the other, at the real cost of maintaining two (or more) copies of the same small piece of logic, and manually keeping any shared bug fixes in sync.

The actual engineering judgment call, applied per shared piece of code: is this logic genuinely stable and unlikely to need a breaking change (good candidate for sharing — most pure utility functions, like parsing or formatting with no business-rule awareness), or does it represent business logic that's likely to evolve independently for different consumers' needs (better candidate for duplication, or at minimum, strict semantic versioning with real consumers pinning specific major versions rather than always taking latest)?

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Sharing a library specifically to enforce "consistency" for logic that different consumers actually have legitimately different needs for — this creates pressure to either break one consumer's expectations (as this demo shows) or add consumer-specific branches inside the shared code, which defeats the purpose of sharing it.
  • Treating a shared internal library as exempt from the versioning discipline Lesson 3 described for service APIs — a breaking change to a widely-used internal package needs the same real-usage-data question ("who still depends on the old behavior?") before it ships everywhere at once.
  • Letting "don't repeat yourself" become an absolute rule rather than a tradeoff — a few lines of duplicated, genuinely independent logic across two services is often cheaper, long-term, than a shared dependency that quietly couples their release schedules together.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a second function to shop_common, format_date(timestamp), used only by newsletter_service.py (not by orders_service.py). Make a breaking change to only format_date, leaving format_price untouched this time. Restart both services and confirm orders_service.py's behavior is completely unaffected — then write one sentence on why this safer case (breaking only a function one consumer actually uses) still doesn't eliminate the deployment coupling: both services still had to be considered, even if only one was actually affected, every time the shared package changes at all.

docs.title: Deployment Strategies for Many Independent Services
What was run
docs.text: A real worker.py service run as three separate real processes (ports 8241-8243) behind a real, hand-written load balancer, lb.py (port 8240), that round-robins across whichever backends last passed a real health check. A real rolling_deploy.py script ran continuous traffic through the load balancer in a background thread while killing and replacing one worker process at a time with a new version, health-checking each replacement before sending it any traffic — a real rolling deployment, not a diagram of one.

docs.title: The rolling deploy, with continuous real traffic running throughout
docs.text:
for port in BACKENDS:
    stop_worker(port)                    # real process kill
    start_worker(port, "v2")             # real process start, new version
    for _ in range(20):                  # real health-check polling before trusting it
        try:
            httpx.get(f"http://localhost:{port}/health", timeout=0.5)
            break
        except httpx.HTTPError:
            time.sleep(0.2)
    httpx.post(f"{LB_URL}/recheck-health")   # only now does the LB route traffic to it again

--- rolling deploy: replacing one worker at a time with v2 ---
  taking 8241 out, deploying v2...
  8241 is back, now serving v2
  taking 8242 out, deploying v2...
  8242 is back, now serving v2
  taking 8243 out, deploying v2...
  8243 is back, now serving v2

--- real results from continuous client traffic during the ENTIRE rolling deploy ---
  ('ok', 'v2'): 63
  ('ok', 'v1'): 42
total requests: 105
total errors (connection/HTTP failures): 0

105 real requests, during the actual window where three processes were individually killed and replaced, with zero errors. The real client thread never saw a failure, because the load balancer never routed traffic to an instance that was down — it only re-added a port to its healthy set after that port's /health endpoint actually responded, as shown above. The version breakdown (42 responses still on v1, 63 already on v2) is itself evidence the deploy genuinely happened gradually: requests were served by a real mix of old and new versions simultaneously throughout the rollout, not an instant all-at-once switch.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A rolling deployment replaces instances of a service one at a time (or in small batches), removing each from the load balancer's rotation, deploying the new version, confirming it's healthy, and only then adding it back — exactly the sequence this demo's script ran for real. Its real strength, measured directly above: it needs no extra infrastructure beyond what's already running (no second full environment), and a failure in the new version is caught on the first replaced instance, while the other two are still serving the old version, limiting the blast radius of a bad deploy to roughly one-third of capacity rather than all of it. Its real cost: for the duration of the rollout, both versions are genuinely live and serving real traffic at the same time, which means the new version must be backward compatible with whatever the old version's clients and data expect — if v2 writes data in a format v1 can't read, and both are live simultaneously, that's a real correctness problem, not just a deployment inconvenience.

Two other strategies worth naming precisely, since "deployment strategy" names get used loosely:

  • Blue-green deployment keeps two complete environments ("blue" = currently live, "green" = the new version, fully deployed but receiving no traffic yet) and switches all traffic from one to the other essentially instantly, usually at the load balancer or DNS level. This avoids the "both versions live simultaneously" window entirely — the switch is atomic — at the cost of needing double the infrastructure capacity during the transition, and a rollback (switching back to blue) is just as instant as the forward switch.
  • Canary deployment, covered in depth with real measured traffic percentages in Level 3, Lesson 6, sends a small, deliberate percentage of traffic to the new version while most traffic stays on the old one — closer in spirit to this lesson's rolling deploy (both versions live at once) but controlled by traffic percentage rather than instance count, which allows a far smaller initial exposure (1% of traffic, say) than a 3-instance rolling deploy's minimum one-third.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Rolling out a change that isn't backward compatible with the previous version, without realizing both versions are genuinely live together during the rollout — this demo's real zero-error result depended entirely on v1 and v2 both being safe to serve the same kind of traffic; a breaking change here would show up as real, intermittent errors precisely correlated with which instance happened to answer each request.
  • Removing an instance from load-balancer rotation and deploying the new version without a real health check gate before adding it back — this demo's explicit polling loop against /health is exactly what prevents routing traffic to a process that's still starting up (common in real frameworks: accepting connections before the application has finished initializing).
  • Treating "zero errors during my test" as proof a rollout is always safe — this demo's worker versions were trivially compatible by design; a real rollout's safety depends on the actual compatibility of what's being deployed, which the load balancer and health checks alone cannot guarantee.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Modify worker.py's v2 behavior to genuinely break backward compatibility — have it return {"version": "v2", "port": PORT, "format": "new"} while v1 still returns the old two-field shape — and modify the continuous traffic client to assert on the exact field set it expects. Re-run the rolling deploy and observe, with real data, exactly how many of the 105-or-so requests would have failed a strict client-side contract check during the mixed-version window, even though the load balancer itself reported zero HTTP-level errors — demonstrating concretely why "the load balancer saw zero errors" and "this deploy was actually safe" are not the same claim.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: Three real services — checkout_gateway.py (port 8250), inventory_service.py (port 8252), and payment_service.py (port 8251) — each writing structured JSON log lines to its own separate log file, all carrying a shared trace_id generated once per checkout at the gateway. A real incident was triggered (payment_service's /charge endpoint made to fail for 5 real seconds), a real checkout was attempted during that window, and the resulting failure was reconstructed into one unified timeline by searching all three separate log files for that one trace ID.

docs.title: Three services, three log files, one shared ID
docs.text:
# obs_lib.py
def log_event(service, trace_id, event, **fields):
    print(json.dumps({"ts": time.time(), "service": service, "trace_id": trace_id, "event": event, **fields}))

# checkout_gateway.py
trace_id = uuid.uuid4().hex[:12]
log_event("checkout-gateway", trace_id, "checkout_started")
httpx.post("http://localhost:8251/charge", headers={"x-trace-id": trace_id}, ...)

curl -s -X POST localhost:8251/simulate-incident/5     # a real 5-second payment outage
curl -s -X POST localhost:8250/checkout -w "\nhttp:%{http_code}\n"
# {"detail":{"trace_id":"c074f12853a9","error":"checkout failed"}}
# http:502

docs.title: Reconstructing the real incident from three separate files
docs.text:
grep "c074f12853a9" gateway.log inventory.log payment.log

t+0.0000s  checkout-gateway   checkout_started
t+0.0102s  inventory-service  reservation_created
t+0.0202s  payment-service    charge_started
t+0.0202s  payment-service    charge_failed        card_network_timeout
t+0.0205s  checkout-gateway   checkout_failed       Server error '504 Gateway Timeout' ...

This is a real, precise, millisecond-level account of exactly what happened to this one request across three separate processes, each with no awareness of the others' internal logs — reconstructed purely because every service tagged its own log lines with the same trace_id. Without that shared ID, these would be three unrelated log files with no way to know which lines belong to the same failed checkout, especially once real traffic volume means hundreds of interleaved requests are hitting all three services at once.

curl -s localhost:8251/metrics
# {"requests_total":3,"errors_total":2}

This real counter adds the piece a single incident's trace can't give you on its own: scale. The trace shows what happened to this one checkout; the metric shows that 2 of the last 3 requests to /charge failed — confirming this wasn't an isolated, one-off failure, which matters for deciding how urgently to respond.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Observability across service boundaries rests on three complementary signals, each answering a different question that the others can't:

  • Logs (what this lesson built) answer "what exactly happened, in detail, for this specific request" — rich, specific, but expensive to query across a large volume of traffic without good correlation (the trace ID).
  • Metrics (the /metrics counter here) answer "how often is this happening, in aggregate, right now" — cheap to query and graph over time, but with none of a single request's specific detail.
  • Traces (built in depth in Level 3, Lesson 8, with real parent-child span timing) answer "where did the time go, structurally, across this one request's hops" — closely related to what this lesson's log correlation reconstructs, but with explicit parent/child span relationships rather than a flat list of log lines a human has to mentally order.

The real, practical lesson this demo makes concrete: none of these three signals alone tells the full incident story. The trace/log timeline above shows precisely what happened to one request; the metric shows it's a real, recurring pattern, not a fluke; neither alone would be as convincing or actionable as having both. The trace_id is the connective tissue that makes the log-based version possible at all — exactly the same context-propagation mechanism Level 3, Lesson 8 built for spans, reused here for log correlation, because it's the same underlying problem: tying together fragments of information that were each generated by a different, independent process with no shared memory.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Logging rich detail in every service without a shared correlation ID connecting them — exactly as Level 3, Lesson 8 warned for traces, this makes a multi-service incident a manual, error-prone correlation exercise across separate files instead of one grep.
  • Having metrics but no logs (or vice versa) for the same failure — a metric telling you "errors are up 40%" with no corresponding detailed log to explain why leaves you stuck at "something is wrong" with no path to "here's the specific cause."
  • Only instrumenting the "normal" success path and leaving failure paths under-logged — this demo's charge_failed event, with its reason field, is exactly the detail that made the reconstructed timeline actionable rather than just "a request to /charge happened and later failed, cause unknown."

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a fourth real signal: a running count of total elapsed time per trace, computed as the difference between the first and last log timestamp sharing a trace_id, aggregated into a simple "average checkout duration, successes vs failures" report queried from the log files directly (no new service needed — just a script reading all three log files, grouping by trace_id). Run several healthy checkouts and one failed one, and confirm your report shows a real, measurable difference between the two groups' durations.

docs.title: Testing Strategies in a Microservices World
What was run
docs.text: A real, trivial unit test file (unit_test_example.py, three tests of a pure apply_discount() function, no network, no services) timed with time.perf_counter(). Then the real integration test suite from Level 2, Lesson 9 (test_saga_consistency.py, which drives four real running services over real HTTP, including the real 2.5-second payment delay added in Level 2, Lesson 8) timed the same way, as a subprocess.

docs.title: The real cost difference, measured
docs.text:
3 unit tests ran in 0.845ms
2 integration tests ran in 5247.1ms

Per test, that's roughly 0.28ms for a unit test versus roughly 2,623ms for an integration test in this real suite — a difference of almost 9,300x. This isn't a contrived example to make a point: the integration tests are genuinely slower because they're doing genuinely more — starting real HTTP connections, waiting on a real payment service that has a real, deliberate 2.5-second delay built into it, and verifying real cross-service state in order_service.py and payment_service.py's actual memory.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This course has already built and run three different kinds of tests, each one deliberately chosen for what it alone could catch:

  • Unit tests (what unit_test_example.py represents) test one function or one small unit of logic, in isolation, with no network calls — fast enough (sub-millisecond here) to run thousands of times per minute, making them the right tool for the bulk of a test suite's pure logic (discount math, validation rules, parsing). They cannot catch anything about how two services behave together, because they never involve two services.
  • Integration tests (test_saga_consistency.py from Level 2, Lesson 9) run real services together and assert on real cross-service outcomes — the only kind of test that could have caught that lesson's missing-refund bug, because the bug lived entirely in the interaction between services, not inside any one of them. The real cost, measured above, is that they're slow, by a factor approaching four orders of magnitude for this suite, and that cost scales with however many services and real network calls a given test chain touches.
  • Contract tests (Level 3, Lesson 9) sit in between: they run against one real service (fast, no multi-service chain) but verify a cross-service concern (does this provider still satisfy what a specific consumer depends on) that a unit test alone can't express.

The practical implication of the real 9,300x gap measured above: a test suite made up entirely of integration tests becomes genuinely too slow to run on every code change, pushing teams toward running it less often (once a day, only before a release) — which delays feedback and makes failures harder to diagnose, since more changes have landed since the last run. The usual answer, often visualized as a "testing pyramid," is proportion: many fast unit tests forming a large base, a smaller number of integration tests covering the specific cross-service interactions that actually need real multi-service verification (not every possible one), and a handful of contract tests per consumer-provider relationship — each tier sized to its real cost, not used uniformly for everything just because it's possible.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Writing an integration test for something a unit test could verify just as well — if a cross-service call could be mocked without losing the thing you're actually testing, the real multi-service cost measured above is being paid for no additional protection.
  • Having no integration tests at all, relying only on fast unit tests — this leaves exactly the class of bug Level 2, Lesson 9 demonstrated (a cross-service interaction bug) with no automated test capable of catching it, regardless of how many unit tests exist.
  • Running the full integration suite on every single local save during development, when its real cost (seconds per test, as measured here) makes that workflow genuinely painful — reserving the full integration suite for CI or pre-merge checks, while developing against fast unit tests locally, is a common, practical compromise.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Write one more integration test against the real saga services (still running from this lesson, or restarted from Level 2, Lesson 4) and time it the same way this lesson did. Then write the equivalent logic as a unit test with the HTTP calls replaced by direct Python function calls or mocks, time that too, and report your own measured ratio between the two — confirming for yourself, with fresh real numbers, that this lesson's 9,300x figure is representative of a real, general pattern and not a one-off result from one specific slow test.

docs.title: Anti-Patterns: the Distributed Monolith & Chatty Services
What was run
docs.text: A real pricing_service.py (port 8261) and a real client script, chatty_checkout.py, computing the exact same checkout total two ways: eight separate, sequential, synchronous HTTP calls (one per cart item) versus one single batched call. Both were timed with time.perf_counter() against the same live service.

docs.title: The real cost of chattiness, measured per request
docs.text:
def chatty_checkout():
    total = 0
    for item_id in ITEMS:                       # 8 items
        r = c.get(f"{PRICING_URL}/price/{item_id}")   # 8 separate round trips, one per item
        total += r.json()["price_cents"]
    return total

def batched_checkout():
    r = c.post(f"{PRICING_URL}/price/batch", json=ITEMS)   # 1 round trip for all 8
    return sum(p["price_cents"] for p in r.json())

chatty checkout  (8 sequential round trips): 40.15ms, total=5332
batched checkout (1 round trip):              9.70ms, total=5332
single-request latency penalty from chattiness: 4.1x

Both return the identical total (5332 cents) — this is purely a latency cost, not a correctness difference. A single user's checkout takes 4.1x longer purely because the service boundary between checkout and pricing was drawn in a way that needs eight sequential round trips to answer one logical question ("what's my cart's total?"), instead of one. This is distinct from Level 1, Lesson 2's N+1 measurement (which was about throughput under load from redundant lookups across many different requests) — this is the same single request's own latency, inflated by how many hops its own logic needs.

docs.title: The second symptom: services that can't actually deploy independently
docs.text: Level 4, Lesson 4 already measured this directly: upgrading one shared package (shop-common) silently changed both orders_service.py's and newsletter_service.py's real API responses at the exact same moment, even though they're two separate deployables with no reason to otherwise coordinate. That's the other defining symptom of a distributed monolith — not excessive chattiness, but services that are deployed separately on paper while actually being unable to change independently in practice.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A distributed monolith is a system split into multiple deployable services that, despite the split, behaves like a monolith in all the ways that matter: changes still need to be coordinated across services, a single logical operation still needs many of them to cooperate closely and synchronously (as measured above), and the system has paid every real cost of being distributed (network latency, partial failure, operational complexity — all covered across Level 1 and Level 3) without gaining the benefits a real microservices split is supposed to provide: independent deployability, independent scaling, and clear ownership boundaries.

The two symptoms demonstrated above are the two most common, concrete ways this shows up: chattiness (measured here — a single operation needs many synchronous hops, each one compounding real latency, exactly the problem Level 1, Lesson 3's sizing heuristics are meant to prevent at design time) and deployment coupling (measured in Lesson 4 — services that are nominally separate but can't actually ship independent changes safely). Either symptom alone is a strong signal the service boundary is drawn wrong, not that "microservices are inherently this way" — a correctly-sized boundary (per Level 1, Lesson 3's heuristics) should need far fewer synchronous hops for its most common operations, and a correctly-isolated boundary (database-per-service from Level 2, Lesson 1, no unnecessarily shared libraries) should allow real independent deploys.

The fix for chattiness specifically, demonstrated directly above, is the same batch-endpoint approach Level 2, Lesson 2 built for a different scenario: the owning service exposes the access pattern its consumers actually need, rather than forcing consumers to assemble it themselves out of many small calls.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating "we have multiple services" as proof of a successful microservices migration, without checking whether any single common operation still requires many synchronous cross-service hops, or whether any two "independent" services actually have to be redeployed together to stay correct.
  • Fixing chattiness by making the many calls asynchronous or parallel instead of reducing the call count — parallel calls reduce wall-clock latency somewhat, but still pay the overhead of N network round trips, N connection setups, and N places a partial failure can occur, compared to one well-designed batched call.
  • Measuring only aggregate system throughput (requests/second) and never a single request's own latency breakdown — this lesson's 4.1x finding is specifically about one user's wait time, which an aggregate throughput number alone can hide.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Change chatty_checkout.py to use httpx's async client and fire all 8 price lookups concurrently instead of sequentially, then re-measure. Confirm the latency gap to the batched version narrows but doesn't disappear entirely — and write down, from the real numbers you measure, how much of the original 4.1x penalty was pure sequential-round-trip latency (fixed by concurrency) versus how much was the fixed per-call overhead of making 8 separate HTTP connections at all (not fixed by concurrency, only by batching).

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: No new experiment — this lesson tallies the real, measured costs from every earlier lesson in this course into one place, as the actual evidence base for the question this lesson is about, rather than restating it as abstract advice.

docs.title: The real bill, so far
docs.text:
Cost Measured in Real number Latency for a simple cross-service join Level 1, Lesson 10 ~13x slower than the monolith's in-process equivalent Redundant lookups without a batch endpoint Level 1, Lesson 2 / Level 2, Lesson 2 5.7x more real HTTP calls than necessary Chattiness in one logical operation Level 4, Lesson 8 4.1x single-request latency penalty New failure modes that didn't exist in the monolith Level 1, Lesson 10 2 new real 503 paths, requiring new handling code Engineering effort to fake a cross-service transaction Level 2, Lessons 4-5 A full saga + outbox implementation, replacing one SQL COMMIT A real eventual-consistency window Level 2, Lesson 8 2.56 real seconds where an order was visibly, correctly PENDING Test suite cost per cross-service test Level 4, Lesson 7 ~9,300x slower per test than an equivalent unit test Deployment coupling despite separate deployables Level 4, Lesson 4 A shared library upgrade broke 2 "independent" services at once

None of these numbers are made up to make a point — they're the actual measurements this course produced along the way, each one a genuine cost of the specific microservices pattern it came from. And every one of them was paired, in its own lesson, with a real benefit that pattern provides when the system actually needs it: independent scaling, independent deployability, fault isolation, team autonomy.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The honest, cumulative conclusion from this table is simple to state and easy to forget in practice: every pattern in this course is a trade, not a free upgrade. A monolith that doesn't have a real, specific scaling problem, a real, specific team-coordination problem, or a real, specific fault-isolation need is paying some subset of the real costs above — slower cross-entity operations, new failure modes, eventual consistency where atomicity used to be free, dramatically more expensive tests — for benefits it isn't actually using yet.

The questions worth asking honestly before splitting, each tied to a real measurement above:

  • Is there an actual, current scaling mismatch between different parts of the system (one part needs 50x the resources of another), or is this hypothetical, "might need it someday" scaling? If hypothetical, the 13x latency cost and the new failure modes from Lesson 10 are being paid for nothing yet.
  • Is there an actual, current team-coordination problem — multiple teams genuinely blocked on each other's release cadence — or is this one team, or a small team that communicates easily? If one team, Conway's Law (Lesson 2) suggests the clean boundary a split promises won't hold anyway, since there's no organizational pressure keeping it clean.
  • Can the team afford the operational and testing overhead — the 9,300x per-test cost difference, the real engineering effort of a saga and an outbox, the discipline of database-per-service — or is this a small team that would spend most of its capacity on this overhead instead of on the product?
  • Does the domain genuinely have the kind of bounded contexts (Level 1, Lesson 2) that justify separate services, or is the "domain" actually small and tightly interrelated enough that forcing a split creates artificial seams with no real counterpart in how the business actually works?

A monolith is not a failure to "modernize" — it's the default, lower-cost starting point that this course's own numbers argue for, right up until a specific, measured problem (not a guess about the future) justifies paying one of the real costs above for a real, needed benefit.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Splitting preemptively, based on anticipated future scale or team growth that hasn't happened yet — every cost in the table above starts accruing immediately, while the anticipated benefit might be months or years away, or might never materialize in the form expected.
  • Treating "everyone else is doing microservices" as evidence for your own system, without checking whether your system has the same scaling, team-size, or fault-isolation needs that made it the right call elsewhere.
  • Assuming a monolith can't be well-modularized — a monolith with clean internal module boundaries, enforced (not just suggested) by code structure, gets much of the "clear ownership" benefit of microservices without paying any of the costs in the table above, and is also the easiest starting point to split later if a real need appears.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Pick a real or hypothetical system you're familiar with. Walk through the four questions above for it, honestly, one at a time, writing a specific answer (not just yes/no) for each — citing an actual current pain point if one exists, or stating plainly "this is hypothetical, not measured" if it doesn't. Based on your four answers alone, not on general enthusiasm for either approach, write one sentence stating whether this system should be a monolith, a few large services, or many small services right now — and what specific, measurable signal would change that answer in the future.

docs.title: Capstone: Build, Break & Observe a Real Multi-Service System
What was run
docs.text: A real four-service saga — order_service.py, payment_service.py, inventory_service.py (all from Level 2, Lesson 4), coordinated by a new capstone_orchestrator.py that combines three patterns built across this entire course: the saga and compensation logic from Level 2, a real pybreaker circuit breaker around the inventory call from Level 3, Lesson 1, and structured, trace-ID-correlated logging from Level 4, Lesson 6. inventory_service.py was killed with a real kill -9 mid-course, three real checkouts were attempted during the outage, and the service was then restarted to observe real recovery.

docs.title: The real failure, fully reconstructed from structured logs
docs.text:
pkill -9 -f "uvicorn inventory_service:app"   # a real, hard kill, no warning
# three real checkouts attempted during the outage...

trace 353b711ce859 (1st failure -- breaker still closed going in):
  saga_started → order_created(id=5) → payment_charged(id=5)
  → inventory_reservation_failed  (breaker_state=closed, reason="Connection refused")
  → compensation_payment_refunded(id=5) → compensation_order_cancelled(id=5)

trace 02fa6ab3c7e6 (2nd failure -- THIS ONE trips the breaker):
  saga_started → order_created(id=6) → payment_charged(id=6)
  → inventory_reservation_failed  (breaker_state=open, reason="Failures threshold reached, circuit breaker opened")
  → compensation_payment_refunded(id=6) → compensation_order_cancelled(id=6)

trace b59721be850f (3rd failure -- breaker already open, call SKIPPED):
  saga_started → order_created(id=7) → payment_charged(id=7)
  → inventory_reservation_failed  (breaker_state=open, reason="Timeout not elapsed yet, circuit breaker still open")
  → compensation_payment_refunded(id=7) → compensation_order_cancelled(id=7)


curl -s localhost:8072/payments   # checked directly against the real payment service, not inferred

{"id": 5, "order_id": 5, "amount_cents": 4000, "status": "REFUNDED"},
{"id": 6, "order_id": 6, "amount_cents": 4000, "status": "REFUNDED"},
{"id": 7, "order_id": 7, "amount_cents": 4000, "status": "REFUNDED"}

All three real charges were really refunded — confirmed independently against Payment Service's own state, not just trusted from the orchestrator's log. And the circuit breaker's real behavior shows exactly across these three traces, in the reason field: the 1st failure is a real network attempt ("Connection refused"), the 2nd is also a real attempt that happens to cross the failure threshold ("Failures threshold reached" — see Level 3, Lesson 1's finding that this specific call is still real), and the 3rd is genuinely skipped with no network call at all ("Timeout not elapsed yet").

# inventory_service.py restarted for real...
curl -s -X POST localhost:8270/checkout -d '{"item":"tripod","amount_cents":4000}'
# {"trace_id":"c06421e6ecf8","saga":"COMPLETED","order_id":8}

A real, clean recovery — no manual intervention needed beyond restarting the dependency; the breaker's own reset_timeout eventually allowed a real probe through, and that probe succeeded.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This capstone is not a new pattern — it's three already-built real patterns, composed, under one real failure, which is exactly what a production incident actually looks like: not one isolated technique being tested, but several working (or failing) together at once. The saga's compensation logic (Level 2) ensured no customer was left charged for an order that never shipped, regardless of how many times the saga failed. The circuit breaker (Level 3) kept the second and third failed attempts from each wasting a full network timeout — visible directly in the real log timestamps, where the 3rd attempt's inventory_reservation_failed event follows its payment_charged event by only ~0.0002 seconds, versus the 1st attempt's real ~16ms network round trip. The structured, trace-correlated logging (Level 4, Lesson 6) is what made it possible to state all of this precisely, from real data, instead of describing it in the abstract.

The real, honest gap this capstone still has, consistent with every earlier lesson's own stated limitations: the orchestrator's saga state lives only in each request's own execution — if the orchestrator process itself had crashed mid-saga (not just the inventory dependency), there's no persistent saga log to resume or verify against, the same limitation Level 2, Lesson 10 named explicitly and left as an acknowledged, real boundary of what this course's scope could cover.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Testing resilience patterns one at a time in isolation and assuming they compose correctly together without ever actually running them together under one real failure, as this capstone did — a circuit breaker and a saga's compensation logic interacting incorrectly (e.g., the breaker's CircuitBreakerError not being caught by the same except clause as the dependency's own exceptions) is a realistic integration bug this kind of combined test would catch and an isolated unit test of either pattern alone would not.
  • Trusting an orchestrator's own response as proof of what really happened, instead of checking the actual downstream state — this capstone's refund confirmation came from querying Payment Service directly, the same discipline Level 2, Lesson 9's consistency tests insisted on.
  • Declaring a system "resilient" after one successful chaos test, without also checking what happens to state left behind by failures that happened before the resilience pattern fully engaged (the 1st trace's real attempt, before the breaker had even tripped yet) — real failures don't wait politely for your protections to be ready.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add persistent saga logging to capstone_orchestrator.py (as sketched, but not fully built, in Level 2, Lesson 10's exercise): write each saga's state to a real SQLite table as it progresses. Then kill the orchestrator process itself (not just inventory) partway through a saga, restart it, and write a small recovery routine that reads any IN_PROGRESS saga from the table and finishes compensating it correctly — closing the one real, acknowledged gap this capstone (and this entire course) leaves open, with your own working code.
